reigns.tagline: The rebel lord who claimed King Solomon as an ancestor
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Rebel who overthrew the Zagwe king
reigns.previously: Aksum is long gone. Zagwe kings rule from Lalibela's rock churches.
paragraphs: Ethiopia's first great kingdom, Aksum, had faded centuries before. In its place the Zagwe kings ruled the northern highlands. The most famous of them, Lalibela, had churches carved straight down into the solid rock. Then, in 1270, a lord from Amhara called Yekuno Amlak rose against them. He beat and killed the last Zagwe king and took the crown for himself.

He needed more than a victory. He claimed to descend from the old kings of Aksum, and through them from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba. Kings who had ruled in between were usurpers, he said. The story was later written down in the Kebra Nagast, the Glory of the Kings, in the early 1300s. His line, the Solomonic dynasty, would hold the throne, on and off, until 1974.

The church backed him. He had studied at the island monastery of Lake Hayq under the abbot Iyasus Moa, and he wrote to the sultan of Egypt asking for a new bishop for his church. He founded the church of Geneta Maryam near Lalibela and died around 1285, leaving the throne to his son.

claims.text: The church got a third of the kingdom's land as its reward for backing Yekuno Amlak.
claims.note: This comes from later monastic tradition, which had every reason to exaggerate its own role. No document from the 1270s records such a deal.

claims.text: Yekuno Amlak really did descend from the kings of Aksum.
claims.note: The family tree was written down by his dynasty's supporters after he took power. Most historians treat it as political legend.

claims.text: He wrote to the Mamluk sultan Baybars asking for a bishop.
claims.note: Egyptian Arabic writers record his letter, sent in the 1270s by way of Yemen.

reigns.hook: Yekuno Amlak is dead. His son Yagbe'u Seyon takes the crown, and a crowd of royal sons and brothers is watching it very closely.

reigns.tagline: The new dynasty's heir who wrote to the sultan of Egypt
reigns.previously: Yekuno Amlak dies around 1285, after founding a new dynasty.
paragraphs: Yekuno Amlak had grabbed the crown. His son Yagbe'u Seyon had to prove the new family could keep it. He ruled as Salomon, a throne name that leaned hard on the claim to King Solomon's blood. The new dynasty was barely fifteen years old, and it needed friends abroad as well as at home.

The church in Ethiopia took its bishop, the abuna, from Egypt, and only the Coptic patriarch in Cairo could send one. That meant asking the Mamluk sultan Qalawun. Yagbe'u Seyon wrote to him, boasting of his power and promising to treat the Muslims of his kingdom well. The letters reached Cairo, but the bishop he wanted was slow to come.
He died in 1294 with several grown sons and no rule about which one should follow him. That was about to become a problem.

claims.text: Yagbe'u Seyon wrote to the Mamluk sultan Qalawun asking for a new bishop.
claims.note: His letters are known from Arabic writers in Egypt, who recorded the exchange; the king's own side of the story does not survive.

claims.text: He promised fair treatment for the Muslims in his lands to win the sultan over.
claims.note: The Arabic accounts say so, but they were written by the sultan's side and may tidy up the king's words.

reigns.hook: Yagbe'u Seyon is dead. His sons are all royal, all grown, and all in the room. The eldest, Senfa Ared, goes first. The others are counting the days.

reigns.tagline: The first brother in a deal to share the crown
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Eldest son of Yagbe'u Seyon to reign
reigns.cameToPower: First turn in the brothers' rota
reigns.previously: Yagbe'u Seyon dies in 1294, leaving sons and no rule for who's next.
paragraphs: Senfa Ared was the first of Yagbe'u Seyon's sons to take the throne. The "IV" in his name comes from the long Ethiopian king lists, which count back through legendary rulers of Aksum. Almost nothing else about him is known: no battles, no buildings, no letters. Just a name and a turn.

The turn is the story. Ethiopian tradition says the brothers struck a bargain: each would reign for a year, then hand over to the next. It sounds like a sensible way to stop royal brothers killing each other. Whether it was a real agreement, or a later story to explain five kings in five years, nobody can say.

claims.text: Yagbe'u Seyon's sons agreed to take the throne for a year each, in turn.
claims.note: Later chronicles and king lists tell it this way. It may be a tidy story laid over a messy run of very short reigns.

claims.text: Senfa Ared reigned for about a year.
claims.note: The king lists give him a single year, but the lists disagree with each other on many early reign lengths.

reigns.hook: Senfa Ared's year is up, and the crown passes on. If the deal holds, it is his brother Hezba Asgad's turn.

paragraphs: Hezba Asgad was the second of Yagbe'u Seyon's sons to wear the crown. That is close to everything we know. His name and his place in the order survive in the king lists, and nothing else: no chronicle, no grant of land, no war.

What is striking is that the handover seems to have worked. In a family with this many princes, brothers usually fought. Here, if the tradition is right, the crown passed calmly from one to the next. The kingdom founded by their grandfather was holding together.

paragraphs: Qedma Asgad, the third brother, is another king known only from the lists. Those lists were copied by monks over centuries, and many copies survive. They often disagree about names, order and reign lengths, especially for the early kings.

Historians piece the early Solomonic kings together by setting the lists side by side and checking them against rare outside records, like letters kept in Egypt. For Qedma Asgad there is no outside record at all. The lists agree he reigned, and roughly when. That is where the trail ends.

reigns.tagline: The last brother, and the end of the deal
reigns.cameToPower: Last turn in the brothers' rota
reigns.previously: Jan Asgad's year is done. The last brother takes his turn.
paragraphs: Saba Asgad was the fifth and last of Yagbe'u Seyon's sons to reign. His year on the throne is as blank in the records as his brothers' years were. The end of it is what matters.

When his turn ended, the crown did not go to one of the brothers' own sons. It went back up a generation, to their uncle Wedem Arad, Yagbe'u Seyon's brother. How that happened is not recorded. It might have been a quiet agreement among the family. It might have been a push.

reigns.tagline: The uncle who sent Ethiopians to meet the Pope
reigns.previously: Saba Asgad's turn ends. The crown jumps back to his uncle.
paragraphs: Wedem Arad, Yagbe'u Seyon's brother, took the crown from his nephews in about 1299 and kept it for some fifteen years. After all the one-year reigns, this was a long, quiet stretch, and the king lists have little to say about it.

One thing stands out. In 1306 an embassy of about thirty Ethiopians reached Europe, looking for allies. A Genoese priest, Giovanni da Carignano, questioned them and wrote down what they said about their country. It was one of the first first-hand reports of Ethiopia to reach Europe.

Tradition also places the start of a grim royal custom here. Spare princes were locked up on a guarded mountain, later Amba Geshen, and let down only when called to be king. When Wedem Arad died, his son Amda Seyon got the crown.

claims.text: Wedem Arad sent an embassy that reached Europe in 1306.
claims.note: Giovanni da Carignano's account survives through a later Italian chronicle. Which king sent the envoys is worked out from the date.

claims.text: Royal princes began to be locked up on a mountain around this time.
claims.note: Ethiopian tradition dates it here. Solid evidence for Amba Geshen as a royal prison comes from the 1400s.

reigns.hook: Wedem Arad dies around 1314. His son Amda Seyon takes the crown, and he has no plans to sit still.

reigns.tagline: The warrior king who doubled his kingdom
reigns.previously: Wedem Arad dies around 1314; his son Amda Seyon takes over.
paragraphs: Amda Seyon spent thirty years at war and nearly always won. He pushed south and west into Gojjam, Damot and Hadiya. To the east lay Ifat and other Muslim states that grew rich on the caravan trade to the Red Sea. He wanted that trade, and he wanted them paying tribute to him.

In 1332 Sabr ad-Din, the sultan of Ifat, rose against him with his allies. Amda Seyon struck east and smashed them. A court writer turned the campaign into a vivid chronicle full of speeches, ambushes and the king charging alone into the enemy. It is one of the earliest royal chronicles we have from Ethiopia.

Monks were less impressed. He took several wives and, they said, women from his father's household too. Holy men from the monasteries told him so to his face and were flogged or sent into exile. By the time he died around 1344 his kingdom was far bigger and far stronger than the one he had inherited.

claims.text: Monks who condemned Amda Seyon's marriages were flogged and exiled.
claims.note: The lives of saints such as Anorewos and Filpos of Debre Libanos tell the story. They are hostile to the king, but the clash is widely accepted.

claims.text: Amda Seyon charged the enemy almost alone and turned the battle.
claims.note: This comes from his own court chronicle, written to glorify him. The campaign is real; the heroics may be polished.

reigns.hook: Amda Seyon is dead. His son Newaya Krestos takes the throne, and the real fights of the next generation will be in the monasteries.

reigns.tagline: The warrior's son who kept the eastern sultans on a leash
reigns.previously: Amda Seyon, the warrior king, dies around 1344.
paragraphs: Amda Seyon had won a huge kingdom. His son Newaya Krestos, who ruled under the throne name Sayfa Arad, had to hold it. He did it for nearly thirty years. In the east, the Muslim sultanate of Ifat still paid tribute and still itched to break free. Sayfa Arad kept it weak by choosing which member of its ruling family got to be sultan, and backing his man with troops.

The bigger trouble was inside the church. The monk Ewostatewos had taught that Christians must keep Saturday holy as well as Sunday. He had left for exile and died abroad, but his followers kept spreading. The bishop and the court refused them ordination, so their monks could not become priests. The quarrel only grew.

claims.text: Sayfa Arad picked and backed his own candidates for the throne of Ifat.
claims.note: Arabic writers and Taddesse Tamrat's study of the period describe him playing rival princes of Ifat against each other.

claims.text: He hit back at Egypt when the Mamluks jailed the Coptic patriarch.
claims.note: An Egyptian chronicler reports the king's anger and reprisals. The story is one-sided and its details are uncertain.

reigns.hook: Newaya Krestos dies around 1372. His son Newaya Maryam takes over a quieter kingdom, and leaves a lot less behind.

reigns.tagline: Ten quiet years while the monks built
reigns.previously: Newaya Krestos dies around 1372; his son takes over.
paragraphs: Newaya Maryam reigned for about ten years, and the chronicles barely notice him. No great war or scandal is pinned to his name. That says something about how secure the kingdom was. A king could now die in his bed and leave the borders where he found them.

The real action was in the monasteries. Monks from Debre Libanos, Lake Hayq and the north fanned out into the highlands, founding houses and preaching in newly conquered lands. When Newaya Maryam died, he had no son to follow him. The crown went to his brother Dawit.

claims.text: Newaya Maryam's reign left almost no record.
claims.note: Historians of the period, Taddesse Tamrat among them, note how little the sources say about these ten years.

claims.text: Newaya Maryam died without a son who could succeed him.
claims.note: That is the usual explanation for the crown passing to his brother. The sources do not say so outright.

reigns.hook: Newaya Maryam is dead, and the crown goes sideways to his brother Dawit. He will rule for thirty years and fill the churches with treasure.

reigns.tagline: The book-loving king, kicked to death by his horse?
reigns.reignEnded: Kicked by his horse, says tradition
reigns.previously: Newaya Maryam dies. His brother Dawit takes the crown.
paragraphs: Dawit I ruled for over thirty years. In the east, the old sultanate of Ifat was reborn as Adal, led by the fierce Sa'ad ad-Din II. Raids flew both ways. Dawit's armies pushed deep into Muslim lands. In the end Sa'ad ad-Din was cornered at the port of Zeila and killed, though when exactly is argued over.

At home Dawit ended the long Sabbath feud. Around 1404 he made peace with the followers of Ewostatewos and let them keep their Saturday holy. Books and relics poured into the churches. Tradition says he got a piece of the True Cross from Egypt. He also sent envoys to Europe, who reached Venice in 1402.
He died around 1413. Tradition says his horse kicked him. He left a crowd of sons, and four of them would be kings.

claims.text: Dawit obtained a fragment of the True Cross from Egypt.
claims.note: Ethiopian tradition says so, and the relic is said to rest at Gishen Maryam. No outside record confirms how it arrived.

claims.text: Dawit died after being kicked by his horse.
claims.note: Later chronicles and king lists report it. No account by an eyewitness survives.

claims.text: Sa'ad ad-Din II was killed at Zeila during Dawit's reign.
claims.note: Some historians date his death to about 1403, under Dawit; others to about 1415, under his son Yeshaq.

reigns.hook: Dawit I is dead, and he has left a crowd of sons. The eldest, Tewodros, gets the crown first. He won't keep it long.

reigns.tagline: A few months on the throne, then centuries of legend
reigns.previously: Dawit I dies around 1413, kicked by his horse, says tradition.
paragraphs: Dawit I's eldest son, Tewodros, took the crown around 1413 and was dead within a year. The chronicles say almost nothing about what he did in that time, and the king lists can't even agree on how many months he had. His brother Yeshaq followed him.

His real career began after he died. Ethiopians came to remember him as a just and godly king, and his name got caught up in prophecy. A text called the Fekkare Iyasus foretold that a king named Tewodros would one day rise to end the country's misery and rule in righteousness. More than four centuries later a self-made warlord, Kassa Hailu, took that name when he was crowned.

claims.text: The prophecy of a coming just king called Tewodros grew out of memories of Tewodros I.
claims.note: A common explanation. When the Fekkare Iyasus took shape, and whom its Tewodros first meant, are both debated.

claims.text: Tewodros I reigned for less than a year.
claims.note: The king lists give him months rather than years, but they differ on the exact length and dates.

reigns.hook: Tewodros is dead after a few months. His brother Yeshaq takes the throne, and he will spend the next fifteen years at war.

reigns.tagline: The king who wrote to Aragon for craftsmen and a bride
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Dawit I; brother of Tewodros I
reigns.previously: Tewodros I dies within a year. His brother Yeshaq takes over.
paragraphs: Dawit's eldest son, Tewodros I, reigned for only a few months before he died. His brother Yeshaq took over and spent fifteen years fighting. In the east the sultans of Adal, heirs to the old rulers of Ifat, kept up a war of raids and counter-raids. Yeshaq struck back hard, and court poets sang about his victories.

In the north-west the Beta Israel, Ethiopia's Jewish community, rose against him. Yeshaq crushed the revolt and took their land. He also looked far beyond his borders. He sent envoys across the Mediterranean to Alfonso V, king of Aragon, asking for skilled craftsmen and proposing a royal marriage. The king of Aragon wrote back, but the grand alliance never happened.

claims.text: Yeshaq ruled that only baptised Christians could inherit land, and the landless Beta Israel came to be called Falasha.
claims.note: This comes from a victory song and later chronicles. The word Falasha probably means exile or landless, but its exact origin is argued over.

claims.text: Yeshaq offered a marriage alliance to Alfonso V of Aragon.
claims.note: Alfonso's surviving letters show the contact was real. The details of the marriage plan rest on a few documents and are not fully clear.

reigns.hook: Yeshaq dies around 1429. His son Andreyas takes the crown, the first of four kings in five years who barely leave a trace.

reigns.tagline: Six months on the throne, then just a name in a list
reigns.previously: Yeshaq dies around 1429 after fifteen years of war.
paragraphs: Yeshaq had spent fifteen years fighting Adal in the east and rebels in the north-west. When he died around 1429, his son Andreyas took the crown. The kingdom was big and full of churches and monasteries, but it had no fixed capital. The royal court was a huge camp of tents that moved from province to province.

And that is nearly all we know. Andreyas reigned for about six months and died. No chronicle says how, or what he did with his short time. His name survives in the king lists, the rolls of rulers copied out by Ethiopian monks. His death opened a run of short reigns that lasted five years.

claims.text: Andreyas reigned for only about six months.
claims.note: The Ethiopian king lists agree on a very short reign, though copies differ on the exact length.

claims.text: The quick turnover after Yeshaq hides a power struggle among Dawit I's descendants.
claims.note: Historians suspect it from the pattern of short reigns. No chronicle of these years survives to say so.

reigns.tagline: The uncle who held on for three whole years
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Dawit I; uncle of Andreyas
reigns.previously: Andreyas dies after six months. The crown goes back a generation.
paragraphs: Dawit I had a lot of sons, and the throne kept coming back to them. Takla Maryam was one, a brother of Tewodros I and Yeshaq. He followed his nephew Andreyas around 1430 and lasted about three years, a long stretch by the standards of this decade. As Negusa Nagast, "King of Kings", he was in theory master of every province and lord.

Royal sons who were not on the throne were dangerous. The kings kept them under guard on Amba Geshen, a flat-topped mountain with sheer cliffs, where they lived in comfort but could not leave. When a king died, the court decided who came down. Takla Maryam died around 1433, and this time the crown went to his own son, Sarwe Iyasus.

claims.text: Takla Maryam was a son of Dawit I and a brother of Zara Yaqob.
claims.note: The king lists name him as a son of Dawit I, and modern histories such as Taddesse Tamrat's accept it.

claims.text: He reigned for about three years.
claims.note: The king lists give roughly three years, but their figures for this decade do not quite agree.

reigns.hook: Takla Maryam is dead. His son Sarwe Iyasus is crowned, and nobody yet knows he has only months to live.

reigns.tagline: A king for a few months, and a mystery ever since
reigns.previously: Takla Maryam dies around 1433 after three years on the throne.
paragraphs: Sarwe Iyasus followed his father Takla Maryam in 1433. He was the third king in about four years, and he did not last either. Within a few months he was dead. Nothing survives to say whether he fell ill, died fighting, or was quietly got rid of by rivals at court.

The silence is the story. Ethiopian royal chronicles, the detailed court histories, are rare before Zara Yaqob's time, and this stretch has none. What we have are the king lists, which give names and lengths of reign and sometimes disagree with each other. After Sarwe Iyasus, his brother Amda Iyasus took the crown.

claims.text: Sarwe Iyasus reigned for only a few months in 1433.
claims.note: The king lists agree on a very short reign; they differ on its exact length.

claims.text: He was murdered by rivals at court.
claims.note: Pure suspicion. Some historians wonder about foul play in such a fast turnover, but no source says how he died.

reigns.hook: Sarwe Iyasus is dead within months. His brother Amda Iyasus steps up, the fourth king since Yeshaq and the last of this unlucky run.

reigns.tagline: Fourth king in five years, and the last of the run
reigns.previously: Sarwe Iyasus dies after a few months. His brother takes the crown.
paragraphs: Amda Iyasus took the crown from his dead brother late in 1433. He was a grandson of Dawit I, and he lasted about seven months before he too died, in 1434. His name means "Pillar of Jesus". That is close to all of him that history kept.

His death left the court stuck. Four kings had come and gone in about five years, and there was no grown prince left in the royal camp. So the nobles looked to Amba Geshen, the prison mountain. Up there, under guard, lived Zara Yaqob, a son of Dawit I in his mid-thirties, who had spent his youth studying and praying in captivity.

claims.text: Amda Iyasus reigned for about seven months.
claims.note: The king lists agree on a very short reign; the number of months varies between copies.

claims.text: Zara Yaqob was brought down from Amba Geshen to take the throne after him.
claims.note: Zara Yaqob's own chronicle tells of his years confined on the royal mountain.

reigns.hook: On the royal mountain, a prince who has spent his youth in captivity hears the guards coming. Zara Yaqob is about to become the most feared king Ethiopia has known.

reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Dawit I; uncle of Amda Iyasus
reigns.cameToPower: Brought down from the royal mountain
reigns.previously: Amda Iyasus dies. The court turns to the prison mountain.
paragraphs: Zara Yaqob spent his youth shut away on the royal mountain of Amba Geshen. He came down around 1434, already in his mid-thirties, sure of his faith and in a hurry. He wrote religious books himself and set out to purify the church. He settled the old Sabbath fight at the Council of Debre Mitmaq around 1450: Saturday and Sunday would both be kept holy.

He was ruthless with anyone who disagreed. A group of monks called the Stephanites refused to bow before images of Mary and before the king. Some were tortured and killed. Abroad, his monks turned up at the Council of Florence in Italy in 1441. At home, in 1445 his army beat the sultan of Adal, Ahmad Badlay, at Gomit.

He grew more suspicious with age and turned on his own family, accusing wives and children of plotting. He built a new capital at Debre Berhan and died there around 1468, feared and admired in equal measure.

claims.text: He founded Debre Berhan, the Mount of Light, after a light was seen in the sky.
claims.note: His chronicle tells it. The light followed the killing of dissenters, and the story was told as a sign of God's approval.

claims.text: He ordered his subjects to bear religious marks or wear amulets showing their faith.
claims.note: His chronicle reports it, but how far the order was enforced, and what the marks were, is uncertain.

claims.text: He had members of his own family beaten after accusing them of plotting.
claims.note: His own court chronicle records it. The deaths that followed are told there too.

reigns.hook: Zara Yaqob is dead. His son Baeda Maryam takes the throne, and his young widow Eleni is about to become the most important person at court.

reigns.tagline: The gentle son who opened his father's prisons
reigns.previously: Zara Yaqob, the iron-fisted reformer, dies around 1468.
paragraphs: Baeda Maryam had good reason to fear his father. Zara Yaqob had his mother, Seyon Mogesa, beaten on suspicion of plotting, and she died of it. The son kept his head down, and when the old king died around 1468 he took the throne at about twenty. Then he set about undoing the terror. He freed prisoners and gave disgraced nobles their lands back.

He kept Queen Eleni, his father's widow, close and honoured her as queen mother. She would be a power at court for half a century. He spent much of his ten years on campaign, against Adal in the east and against the Dobe'a, a stubborn lowland people. He died in November 1478 and was buried at Atronsa Maryam, a church he had founded. His son Eskender was seven.

claims.text: Baeda Maryam's mother died after Zara Yaqob had her beaten.
claims.note: Zara Yaqob's own chronicle records the beatings of family members accused of plotting.

claims.text: He freed many of his father's prisoners and restored disgraced nobles.
claims.note: His chronicle reports the pardons, and historians read them as a deliberate break with the old regime.

reigns.hook: Baeda Maryam dies in 1478. His son Eskender is a little boy of seven, so the lords, the churchmen and Queen Eleni start fighting over who really rules.

reigns.tagline: The boy king who welcomed Portugal's secret agent
reigns.cameToPower: Succeeded his father as a child
reigns.previously: Baeda Maryam dies in 1478, leaving a seven-year-old son.
paragraphs: Eskender was seven when his father died. He was crowned, and the grown-ups took over. Queen Eleni and the great officials ran the government, while rival lords fought for control of the boy. The feuds were bitter and sometimes deadly. Eskender grew up in the middle of them and in his teens began to rule in his own right.

In about 1493 a remarkable visitor reached his camp. Pêro da Covilhã had been sent by King João II of Portugal to find Prester John, the Christian king of European legend. Eskender received him kindly. Then, in May 1494, the young king died at twenty-two, and his successors would not let the Portuguese go home. Eskender's small son Amda Seyon was crowned next.

claims.text: Eskender would have let Pêro da Covilhã go home, but died first.
claims.note: Francisco Álvares heard this from Covilhã himself in the 1520s. We only have Covilhã's side.

claims.text: Eskender was killed on campaign against Adal.
claims.note: Accounts differ: some say he died fighting, others that one of his own men killed him. The date is better known than the cause.

claims.text: His regent Amda Mikael was put to death by a rival faction.
claims.note: The chronicle tradition records his fall, but the details and the date are unclear.

reigns.hook: Eskender is dead at twenty-two. His son Amda Seyon is about six, and the court factions are already fighting over him.

reigns.tagline: A six-year-old king caught between grown-up factions
reigns.previously: Eskender dies young in 1494. His little son is crowned.
paragraphs: Amda Seyon II shared his name with the great warrior king of the 1300s, but he never got the chance to live up to it. He was about six when his father Eskender died in 1494. One group of courtiers put him on the throne, hoping to rule through him. Other lords had their own plans.

Within months the boy was dead, a child swallowed by a grown-up power struggle. When the fighting was over, the winners passed over Eskender's line altogether. They went back to Amba Geshen and brought down Na'od, a son of Baeda Maryam and the dead boy's uncle.

claims.text: Amda Seyon II was killed in the fighting between court factions.
claims.note: Later sources say he was killed; how and by whom is not clear.

claims.text: He reigned for only a few months in 1494.
claims.note: The king lists agree on a reign of months, not years.

reigns.hook: The boy king is gone. The court fetches his uncle Na'od down from the royal mountain, and old Queen Eleni is still there to guide him.

reigns.previously: Little Amda Seyon II dies within months, lost in a court feud.
paragraphs: Na'od had spent years under guard on Amba Geshen when the court came for him in 1494. He was a son of Baeda Maryam and the uncle of the dead boy king. Queen Eleni, by now a grand old figure, stood beside him. Pêro da Covilhã was still at court, given land and a wife but never allowed to leave.

Na'od ruled for fourteen years, with frontier wars against the Muslim states to the east and their raiders. He began a great church, Mekane Selassie, so rich in gold that it amazed the army that later burned it. On 31 July 1508 he was killed fighting Muslim forces. His son Lebna Dengel was about eleven.

claims.text: Na'od refused to let Pêro da Covilhã leave Ethiopia.
claims.note: Covilhã told Francisco Álvares so in the 1520s, and Álvares wrote it down.

claims.text: Na'od founded the church of Mekane Selassie.
claims.note: Ethiopian tradition credits him, with his son finishing it. The Futuh, the chronicle of Ahmad's war, describes its gold before it was burned.

reigns.hook: Na'od falls in battle in 1508. His son Lebna Dengel is just a boy. Queen Eleni steps in to steer, and in Adal a storm is building.

reigns.tagline: Prester John himself, until the storm came from Adal
reigns.reignEnded: Died on the run near Debre Damo
reigns.previously: Na'od falls in battle. Old Queen Eleni is still pulling the strings.
paragraphs: Lebna Dengel took the throne as a boy, with the shrewd old Queen Eleni guiding the regency. Europe had long dreamed of Prester John, a mighty Christian king somewhere beyond the Muslim world. Ethiopia's emperor fitted the bill. In 1520 a Portuguese embassy finally arrived, and its chaplain Francisco Álvares spent six years at court and wrote it all up.

Lebna Dengel had won battles young and felt safe, so he sent the Portuguese home without the alliance Eleni had wanted. Then Ahmad ibn Ibrahim of Adal, called Gragn, "the Left-handed", marched in. To many Somalis and Muslims he is a hero to this day. He crushed the imperial army at Shimbra Kure in 1529, and for over a decade his forces swept the highlands, burning churches and monasteries.

The King of Kings (Negusa Nagast) became a hunted man, moving from mountain to mountain while his family was captured or killed. He sent a desperate plea to Portugal for guns. Help was coming, but too late for him. He died in September 1540 near Debre Damo, a cliff-top monastery you can only reach by climbing a rope.

claims.text: Lebna Dengel was the real "Prester John" of European legend.
claims.note: The Prester John myth began in the 12th century and drifted from Asia to Africa. The Portuguese simply pinned it on whoever ruled Ethiopia.

claims.text: Lebna Dengel snubbed the Portuguese alliance because he thought he no longer needed it.
claims.note: Álvares's account shows a cool, haughty reception. Historians read it as overconfidence after early victories, but his motives are guessed at.

claims.text: Pêro da Covilhã, the Portuguese traveller held at court since about 1494, was still alive when Álvares arrived.
claims.note: Álvares met him and recorded his story first-hand.

reigns.hook: The old emperor is dead in the mountains. His young son Gelawdewos inherits a burned kingdom, and four hundred Portuguese musketeers are already at sea.

reigns.previously: Lebna Dengel dies a fugitive. Adal holds most of the highlands.
paragraphs: Gelawdewos (Claudius to the Europeans) inherited a crown and not much else. In 1541 about 400 Portuguese musketeers landed at Massawa under Christovão da Gama, son of the explorer Vasco da Gama. They won early fights, but in 1542 Ahmad, reinforced by Ottoman gunners, routed them. Da Gama was captured and executed.

Gelawdewos joined the survivors, and in February 1543 they met Ahmad at Wayna Daga. Ahmad was shot dead and his army broke. To Christians it was a deliverance; to many Muslims and Somalis Ahmad remains a great hero. Gelawdewos spent years rebuilding, winning back lords who had changed sides and churches that had changed hands.

The Portuguese wanted payment in souls. Jesuits arrived to bring Ethiopia under Rome, and Gelawdewos politely refused, writing a confession of his Orthodox faith. In 1559 Nur ibn Mujahid, emir of Harar, who had married Ahmad's widow, marched against him. Gelawdewos fell in battle.

claims.text: A Portuguese musketeer named João de Castilho fired the shot that killed Ahmad.
claims.note: Portuguese accounts claim the kill for their own side. Who exactly shot him at Wayna Daga can't be pinned down.

claims.text: Ahmad's widow Bati del Wambara made avenging her husband a condition of marrying Nur.
claims.note: A popular story in Harar tradition and later retellings; contemporary sources are thin.

claims.text: Gelawdewos wrote a defence of the Ethiopian faith against the Jesuits.
claims.note: The "Confession of Claudius" (1555) survives and was printed in Europe.

reigns.previously: Gelawdewos falls fighting the emir of Harar in 1559.
paragraphs: Menas, a son of Lebna Dengel, spent the war years as a prisoner of Ahmad ibn Ibrahim. He was kept alive as a valuable hostage. After Ahmad was killed in 1543 his own son fell into Christian hands, and Gelawdewos swapped him for Menas. The royal family celebrated for days.

Sixteen years later Gelawdewos was dead and Menas was King of Kings. He campaigned against the Beta Israel in Semien and packed the Jesuit bishop Andrés de Oviedo off to a village near Adwa. About a year in, the Bahr Negash Yeshaq, lord of the coastal north (his title means "king of the sea"), rebelled and named a royal bastard called Tazkaro as king.

Menas beat Yeshaq and in July 1561 crushed Tazkaro's last backers. Tazkaro was thrown off a cliff on his orders. But Yeshaq came back with Ottoman troops from Massawa and beat Menas in April 1562. The emperor was still trying to recover when he died early in 1563.

claims.text: Ahmad sent Menas to the ruler of Yemen as part of a gift in return for military help.
claims.note: Reported in some sources and by the Jesuit Jerónimo Lobo, who added that Menas turned Muslim in captivity. Neither is confirmed.

claims.text: Menas had the pretender Tazkaro thrown from the rock of Lamalmon.
claims.note: From the royal chronicle tradition, which James Bruce followed.

claims.text: Menas had all his brother's faults and none of his virtues.
claims.note: The verdict of Jerónimo Lobo, a Jesuit writing decades later about a king who had exiled his order's bishop.

reigns.hook: Menas dies with the rebels still in the field. His son Sarsa Dengel, barely a teenager, inherits a war on the coast and much more besides.

reigns.previously: Menas dies in 1563, his war with the coastal rebels unfinished.
paragraphs: Gelawdewos's brother Menas ruled from 1559 to 1563, fighting rebels most of the time. Then his young son Sarsa Dengel took over. The boy grew into a tough campaigner, which was just as well, because trouble came from every side.

From the south the Oromo were moving north in great waves, settling lands left empty after the wars with Adal. The monk Bahrey wrote a short, sharp history of them in 1593, wondering why his own people were losing. On the Red Sea coast the Ottomans held Massawa and were pushing inland; Sarsa Dengel beat them. In the Semien mountains he fought the Beta Israel, Ethiopia's Jews, who resisted fiercely from their peaks.
He spent over thirty years in the saddle and held the kingdom together. He died in 1597, and his chronicler blamed a fever. He left a young son and plenty of grown-up relatives with ideas.

claims.text: Sarsa Dengel died after eating fish from a river while on campaign.
claims.note: Later accounts link his fatal fever to the fish. It may be a chronicler's explanation after the fact.

claims.text: Bahrey's "History of the Galla" was written in 1593.
claims.note: The text dates itself and survives in several manuscripts.

claims.text: Beta Israel fighters threw themselves off cliffs rather than be captured.
claims.note: Stories of mass suicide in the Semien campaigns come from the royal chronicle and later tradition; details are hard to check.

paragraphs: Sarsa Dengel left plenty of grown relatives and one young son. The great nobles picked the son, Yaqob, about seven years old, because a child could not tell them what to do. He took the throne name Malak Sagad, his father's own. For six years the lords ran the kingdom in his name and did very nicely out of it.

Then Yaqob grew up. In his early teens he started acting like a real emperor, and the nobles did not like it. In 1603 they deposed him and sent him off to Enarya, a far-off land in the south-west. In his place they crowned his cousin Za Dengel, a nephew of Sarsa Dengel.

claims.text: Yaqob was deposed because he tried to rule for himself.
claims.note: That is how the chronicles and Jesuit writers explain it; the nobles' own motives are not recorded.

claims.text: He was exiled to Enarya, in the far south-west.
claims.note: The royal chronicles and Pedro Páez both record his exile there.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who flirted with Rome and paid for it
reigns.previously: Yaqob is deposed and exiled. His cousin Za Dengel is crowned.
paragraphs: Za Dengel was a nephew of Sarsa Dengel, and he turned out sharp, curious and keen on reform. He soon met Pedro Páez, a Spanish Jesuit who reached Ethiopia in 1603 after years as a captive in Arabia. Páez learned Ge'ez, the church language, and charmed the court. Za Dengel listened, and began talking of joining the Church of Rome.

For the church this was treason. The Abuna Petros, head of the Ethiopian church, released Za Dengel's subjects from their oaths of loyalty. The nobles, already uneasy about his reforms, rose in revolt under the general Za Selassie. On 24 October 1604 the emperor met the rebels in battle and was killed. The lords sent to Enarya to fetch Yaqob back.

claims.text: Za Dengel secretly promised to become a Catholic.
claims.note: Jesuit letters say so with obvious enthusiasm. Ethiopian sources mainly record the backlash.

reigns.cameToPower: Recalled from exile by the lords

reigns.previously: Za Dengel is killed in battle. Yaqob is brought back from exile.
paragraphs: Yaqob came back from Enarya older and wiser, but his position was weak. The lords who had thrown him out now needed him, and they had not suddenly become loyal. Worse, he was not the only claimant. Susenyos, another royal cousin who had grown up among the Oromo and led his own war band, had already declared himself emperor.

The two cousins fought it out for nearly three years. On 10 March 1607 their armies met at Gol. Yaqob was killed, and so was the Abuna Petros, who had stood with him. Susenyos was now the only emperor left standing.

claims.text: Yaqob's body was never found, and pretenders later used his name.
claims.note: Ethiopian sources say the body was not identified, and men claiming to be Yaqob did appear later. Whether he really survived is another matter.

claims.text: The Abuna Petros died at Gol fighting on Yaqob's side.
claims.note: Recorded in the chronicle of Susenyos and by Pedro Páez.

reigns.hook: Yaqob is dead at Gol. The winner, Susenyos, grew up a captive among the Oromo and a bandit chief. Now he is emperor, and his Jesuit friend Páez has big plans.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who turned Catholic and set his realm on fire
reigns.cameToPower: Killed Yaqob at the battle of Gol
reigns.reignEnded: Abdicated for his son, then died
reigns.previously: Yaqob dies at the battle of Gol. His cousin Susenyos takes the crown.
paragraphs: Susenyos had a wild youth. Carried off as a boy by Oromo raiders, he lived among them, then roamed as a freebooter with his own band. He knew how to fight and how to win people over. Once emperor, he made friends with the Jesuit Pedro Páez, a clever builder and a patient talker.

Páez won him over. Susenyos declared himself a Catholic, publicly in 1622. Páez died that year, and his successors were far less tactful. In 1626 the Portuguese patriarch Afonso Mendes arrived and ordered Roman ways: new rites, new feast days, priests re-ordained, even rules on circumcision. To most Ethiopians this was an attack on who they were.

Revolt after revolt followed. In 1632 Susenyos won a bloody battle, and the sight of thousands dead seems to have broken him. He announced that people could return to their old faith, handed power to his son Fasilides, and died a few months later.

claims.text: Pedro Páez built Susenyos a stone palace at Gorgora on Lake Tana.
claims.note: Jesuit accounts credit Páez with the building. How much was his own design is debated, and the ruins are hard to date.

claims.text: After the last battle, Fasilides showed his father the dead and said they were his own subjects.
claims.note: A famous scene in later retellings; the exact words are a storyteller's.

claims.text: Susenyos publicly professed the Catholic faith in 1622.
claims.note: Recorded by the Jesuits and in his royal chronicle.

reigns.hook: Susenyos is dead and the Catholic experiment with him. His son Fasilides has scores to settle, starting with the Jesuits.

reigns.cameToPower: His father abdicated in his favour
reigns.previously: Susenyos gives up on Rome, hands over to his son and dies.
paragraphs: Fasilides moved fast. The Catholic patriarch Afonso Mendes and the Jesuits were thrown out, and those who tried to sneak back faced death. He even made deals with the Ottoman governors on the coast to stop missionaries landing. The Orthodox church was back in charge, and Europe was kept at arm's length for generations.

For centuries the emperors had lived in moving tent cities. Fasilides settled down. From about 1636 he made Gondar, north of Lake Tana, his permanent capital and built a stone castle with towers and battlements. His successors added more, and the walled royal compound, Fasil Ghebbi, is now a World Heritage Site. A pool outside town is still called Fasilides' Bath.
Gondar grew into a busy city of churches, markets and courtiers. Fasilides ruled for 35 years and died in 1667, leaving his son Yohannes a settled capital and a church sure of itself.

claims.text: Fasilides had his own brother put to death.
claims.note: Reported in chronicles and later histories amid the purge of Catholic supporters; the details and the motive are unclear.

claims.text: Fasilides built the bathing pavilion now called Fasilides' Bath.
claims.note: Tradition gives it his name, but some scholars date the building later in the Gondar period.

claims.note: UNESCO lists it as Fasil Ghebbi, Gondar Region.

reigns.hook: The castle-builder is dead. His son Yohannes is a stern and pious man, and he has firm ideas about who should live where in Gondar.

reigns.tagline: The strict churchman who drew lines across Gondar
reigns.previously: Fasilides dies after 35 years, leaving Gondar a real capital.
paragraphs: Yohannes was devout to the bone. Soon after taking over he ordered Muslims and the last Catholics, mostly descendants of the Portuguese, to live apart from Christians. Gondar's Muslims got their own quarter below the city, where they did much of the trading.

He also refereed the church's fiercest argument of the day: exactly how Christ's divine and human natures were united. Rival schools of monks shouted it out at councils in front of the emperor, and Yohannes leaned on them to agree. They didn't, not for another two centuries. He died in 1682, and his son Iyasu stepped up.

claims.text: Yohannes ordered Muslims and remaining Catholics to live apart from Christians.
claims.note: Recorded in his royal chronicle; Gondar's separate Muslim quarter grew from it.

reigns.hook: Yohannes dies, and his son Iyasu inherits a quiet capital. Iyasu will not be quiet. He will become the greatest of all the Gondar emperors.

reigns.tagline: Gondar's greatest emperor, betrayed by his own son
reigns.reignEnded: Murdered on a Lake Tana island
reigns.previously: Pious Yohannes I dies. His son Iyasu takes the throne at Gondar.
paragraphs: Iyasu was the last truly powerful emperor at Gondar. He led armies south and west, collected tribute, and kept the great lords in line. He called church councils to settle the argument over Christ's nature and tried to make the decisions stick. People called him Iyasu the Great.

He built too. His church of Debre Berhan Selassie, "Light of the Trinity", still stands in Gondar, its ceiling covered in rows of painted winged angels' faces. In 1699 a French doctor, Charles Poncet, came to treat him for a skin complaint and left one of the few outside descriptions of the court, all gold, velvet and ceremony.

Late in life Iyasu grew weary. He withdrew to an island in Lake Tana, and nobles crowned his son Tekle Haymanot in his place. In 1706 the old emperor was murdered on the island, and the son's party got the blame.

claims.text: In 1691 Iyasu had the Ark of the Covenant's casket opened at Aksum and spoke to it.
claims.note: The visit is told in his royal chronicle and retold by James Bruce; what was in the casket is a matter of faith.

claims.text: The famous angel ceiling at Debre Berhan Selassie dates from Iyasu's time.
claims.note: The church was founded under Iyasu, but it was damaged and partly rebuilt later, and the paintings may be 18th-century.

claims.text: Iyasu retired to the island after the death of his favourite companion.
claims.note: The chronicle links his withdrawal to grief; modern historians also see a court plot.

reigns.hook: The great Iyasu is dead, killed for his son. That son, Tekle Haymanot, now has the crown to himself. Gondar is about to give him a nickname he will never shake.

reigns.tagline: Crowned while his father lived, cursed once he died
reigns.previously: Iyasu the Great is murdered on his island. His son gets the blame.
paragraphs: In 1706 the old emperor Iyasu I left Gondar for an island in Lake Tana, and a group of nobles crowned his son Tekle Haymanot in his place. A father alive and a son on the throne was a recipe for trouble. Within months Iyasu was dead, cut down on his island, and everyone believed the order had come from the new emperor's side.

Gondar never let him forget it. People called him Irgum, "the Accursed". His reign was short and jumpy, a young man watching for the next plot. He was right to worry. On 30 June 1708, out hunting, he was set upon and killed by conspirators. He was about 24. The crown passed to his uncle Tewoflos, Iyasu's brother, who had scores to settle.

claims.text: Tekle Haymanot ordered his father's murder.
claims.note: The court and the chronicles blamed him and his circle. Some historians put more weight on his mother Malakotawit and her allies, with the son as their figurehead.

claims.text: He was known as Irgum, "the Accursed", for the killing of his father.
claims.note: The nickname appears in the regnal lists and the standard histories of Gondar.

reigns.hook: The parricide is dead in the hunting field. His uncle Tewoflos takes the crown, and he wants to know exactly who killed his brother Iyasu.

reigns.tagline: The uncle who came back to avenge his brother
reigns.cameToPower: Raised up after his nephew's murder
reigns.previously: Tekle Haymanot, "the Accursed", is murdered on a hunting trip.
paragraphs: Tewoflos was Iyasu the Great's brother, and he took the throne with one job in mind. The men and women blamed for Iyasu's murder were hunted down and put to death. The most famous victim was Malakotawit, Iyasu's queen and Tekle Haymanot's mother, whom many at court saw as the brain behind the whole affair.

Revenge took up most of his three years. Gondar's great families watched nervously, wondering who would be next. When Tewoflos died in October 1711, the nobles did something new. Iyasu still had grown sons, but instead of picking one of them, the court chose a man from outside the royal male line.

claims.text: Tewoflos had Queen Malakotawit executed for her part in Iyasu's murder.
claims.note: The chronicle tradition says so and later histories repeat it. How far she really planned the killing is impossible to check.

claims.text: The nobles passed over Iyasu's sons because they feared revenge.
claims.note: The usual explanation in modern histories: many courtiers had backed Tekle Haymanot. It is an inference from what happened, not a recorded reason.

reigns.hook: Iyasu's sons are waiting in the wings, but the court has other ideas. The next emperor is a powerful courtier whose royal blood comes only through his mother. His name is Yostos.

reigns.tagline: The outsider who broke the Solomonic chain
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Grandson of Yohannes I via his mother
reigns.previously: Avenging Tewoflos dies. The court passes over Iyasu's sons.
paragraphs: For four centuries the emperors claimed to descend, father to son, from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba. Yostos broke the chain. His father was a court official and his royal blood came only through his mother. To the old families he was a usurper, however he dressed it up.

He tried to look outward. In 1712 three Catholic friars from Europe reached Gondar, and Yostos received them and let them stay. That was a risky move in a kingdom that still remembered the bitter fight over Catholicism a century earlier. Early in 1716 he fell seriously ill. Supporters of Iyasu's son Dawit seized the moment, and Yostos was pushed aside and died soon after.

claims.text: Yostos was the first emperor from outside the Solomonic male line.
claims.note: Regnal lists and the standard histories agree that he descended from the dynasty only through his mother.

claims.text: The three Franciscan friars he welcomed were stoned to death soon after his fall.
claims.note: Their deaths at Gondar in March 1716 are recorded by the Catholic Church, which beatified their leader Liberatus Weiss in 1988.

reigns.hook: Yostos is finished. Iyasu's son Dawit is fetched to Gondar, and the friars Yostos protected are about to discover how little his protection is worth.

reigns.reignEnded: Sudden death, said to be poison
reigns.previously: Yostos falls gravely ill and is shoved off the throne.
paragraphs: Dawit's reign opened with a killing. In March 1716 the three Catholic friars whom Yostos had sheltered were dragged out and stoned to death in Gondar. The message was clear: the old faith was back in charge, and foreigners preaching Rome were not welcome.

The church itself was split down the middle. Rival schools of monks argued over exactly how Christ was anointed by the Holy Spirit, and the argument was about power as much as theology. Dawit took sides, and the quarrel turned bloody, with monks of the losing party killed by royal troops. In May 1721 the emperor died suddenly, still in his twenties. The court said poison.

claims.text: Dawit was poisoned.
claims.note: His sudden death was blamed on poison at the time. Nothing proves it, and a plot was the usual explanation for any royal death in Gondar.

claims.text: Royal troops massacred monks during the doctrinal dispute.
claims.note: The chronicles and church tradition describe killings, especially of monks linked to Debre Libanos. The numbers and who gave the order are uncertain.

claims.text: Dawit III built a great hall in Gondar's royal compound.
claims.note: A hall in the Fasil Ghebbi is traditionally attributed to him and still carries his name.

reigns.hook: Another emperor dead before his time. The last grown son of Iyasu standing is Bakaffa, a hard, suspicious man who trusts nobody, and maybe he's right not to.

reigns.tagline: The stern emperor who ruled Gondar by fear
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Iyasu I, brother of Dawit III
reigns.previously: Dawit III dies suddenly. The court whispers about poison.
paragraphs: After fifteen years of murder and coups, Bakaffa decided the answer was fear. He watched the nobles closely, struck first when he smelled a plot, and kept the great families off balance. It worked, more or less. Gondar had its first stretch of grim calm since Iyasu's day.

He also built. His palace and a banqueting hall went up inside the royal compound, adding to the castles of his ancestors. He married Mentewab, a young noblewoman from Qwara, west of Lake Tana, and in 1723 she gave him a son, Iyasu. In his last years Bakaffa was often ill. He died in September 1730, and his heir was a small boy.

claims.text: Bakaffa wandered his kingdom in disguise and met his wife Mentewab that way.
claims.note: A romantic court story about the match. The chronicles show a political marriage that tied the crown to a strong family from Qwara.

claims.text: Bakaffa had his own chronicle written.
claims.note: His reign is covered by a royal chronicle, published by Ignazio Guidi in 1903 together with those of Yohannes I and Iyasu I.

reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Bakaffa and his widow

paragraphs: Mentewab, baptised Walatta Giyorgis, came from Qwara, west of Lake Tana. When her husband died she did something new. She had herself crowned beside her son as co-ruler, and for the next quarter of a century she was the power in Gondar. Her brother and other Qwara kin filled the top jobs at court, which the older noble families hated.

She built on a grand scale. Her palace and church at Kuskuam, just outside the city, became her own little court. Iyasu grew up but never really took the reins. He loved the hunt and fine buildings, and left the business of ruling to his mother.

He did go to war once in a big way. In 1744 he marched on the kingdom of Sennar in Sudan, and his army was badly beaten. In 1755 he died suddenly, still young. His son Iyoas was a child, so Mentewab carried on.

claims.text: Iyasu cared more for hunting and building than for ruling.
claims.note: This is the picture painted by the chronicles and by James Bruce, who heard it from courtiers. It may be unfair to a man whose mother held the real power.

claims.text: Iyasu was poisoned.
claims.note: Rumours blamed rivals at court for his sudden death in 1755. There is no solid evidence either way.

claims.text: Mentewab was crowned as co-ruler with her son.
claims.note: Recorded in the royal chronicle of Iyasu II; the standard histories accept it.

reigns.previously: Iyasu II dies young. Mentewab keeps the regency for his little son.
paragraphs: Iyoas had two families, and they couldn't stand each other. On one side stood his grandmother Mentewab and her Qwara kin. On the other stood his mother Wubit, an Oromo noblewoman from the Yejju and Wollo country, whose relatives arrived in Gondar with their own soldiers. As the boy grew up he leaned to his mother's side.

The old nobles looked for a strongman to fix things, and they found one in Ras Mikael Sehul, the hard old lord of Tigray. A Ras was a top-rank noble. Mikael was invited to Gondar to help and stayed to rule.

In 1769 Mikael had Iyoas strangled. He put an elderly prince on the throne, who was dead within months. From now on emperors would be made and unmade by warlords. The crown kept its glamour, but the power had gone.

claims.text: Iyoas preferred to speak Oromo at court.
claims.note: Reported by James Bruce and repeated by later historians. It reflects how his enemies saw him and may be exaggerated.

claims.text: Iyoas was killed on the orders of Ras Mikael Sehul.
claims.note: The royal chronicle and Bruce, who arrived in Ethiopia that year, agree that Mikael was behind it.

reigns.previously: Iyoas is strangled on the orders of Ras Mikael Sehul.
paragraphs: Gondar's spare princes were kept on Wehni, a steep flat-topped mountain where they were guarded for life. Yohannes, a son of Iyasu I, had spent most of his roughly seventy years there. In 1769, after Iyoas was strangled, Ras Mikael Sehul needed a royal face and sent for the old man.

This was the start of what Ethiopians call the Zemene Mesafint, the Era of the Princes, named after the Bible's line about days when Israel had no king. Gondar still had emperors, but warlords made and broke them. Yohannes was the first such puppet, and he did not last. In October 1769 he died, five months in, and many believed Mikael had poisoned him.

claims.text: Yohannes II was poisoned on Mikael Sehul's orders.
claims.note: James Bruce, who reached Ethiopia that year, and court gossip pointed at Mikael. There is no firm proof.

claims.text: Yohannes had lost a hand years earlier, which should have barred him from the throne.
claims.note: Reported in later accounts. A maimed man was normally unfit to reign in Ethiopia, which makes the story notable, but it is hard to confirm.

reigns.hook: One old puppet down. Mikael Sehul doesn't bother looking far for the next: he crowns Yohannes's teenage son, Tekle Haymanot, and keeps the real power for himself.

reigns.tagline: A teenage puppet, a warlord and a tall Scot
reigns.previously: Old Yohannes II dies after five months. Poison, people say.
paragraphs: Tekle Haymanot II was about fifteen when Ras Mikael Sehul put the crown on his head. Mikael was the hard old lord of Tigray, now running Gondar as regent; a Ras was a top-rank noble. The young emperor did as he was told.

Early in 1770 a visitor turned up. James Bruce, a very tall Scot hunting for the source of the Nile, came to court and stayed. He doctored royal relatives, rode with the army, and made friends with Mikael's wife, Esther, daughter of the old empress Mentewab. Then Mikael and the emperor marched off to fight rebels, and behind their backs the nobles in Gondar crowned someone else.

claims.text: James Bruce served at Tekle Haymanot II's court and was given a court title.
claims.note: Bruce describes it in his Travels, and the outline of his stay is accepted, though he liked to make himself the hero of every scene.

claims.text: Bruce cured members of the royal family of smallpox.
claims.note: Bruce's own claim. He did practise as a doctor at court, but how much he really cured is his word alone.

reigns.hook: While the emperor is away at war, Gondar's nobles crown a rival called Susenyos. Mikael Sehul hears the news, and turns his army around.

reigns.tagline: Crowned behind a warlord's back, gone by Christmas
reigns.previously: Mikael Sehul takes young Tekle Haymanot II off to war.
paragraphs: With Ras Mikael and the young emperor away fighting, the nobles left in Gondar saw their chance. They crowned Susenyos, who claimed to be a son of Iyasu II, though not by his wife. It was a gamble that Mikael would lose his war and never come back.

He came back. By the end of 1770 Mikael's army was in Gondar again, and the men who had cheered the new emperor ran or paid for it. Susenyos was overthrown after about four months. The usual account says he was later put to death. Tekle Haymanot II was put back on the throne, still Mikael's puppet.

claims.text: Susenyos II was an illegitimate son of Iyasu II.
claims.note: That was his claim and the regnal lists accept him as royal, but his birth cannot be checked.

claims.text: Susenyos II was executed after Mikael Sehul retook Gondar.
claims.note: Reported in the standard lists and histories; details of how and when differ.

reigns.hook: Mikael is back in Gondar and Tekle Haymanot II is back on the throne. But the great lords are tired of the old Tigrayan, and they are gathering their armies.

reigns.tagline: The puppet loses his puppeteer and tries to rule
reigns.cameToPower: Put back by Ras Mikael Sehul
reigns.previously: Mikael Sehul storms back into Gondar. Susenyos II is finished.
paragraphs: Back on the throne, Tekle Haymanot watched his patron fall. In 1771 a coalition of lords from Gojjam, Begemder and the west beat Mikael Sehul's army. The old Ras was taken prisoner and in the end sent home to Tigray, where he lived out his days. Bruce left Ethiopia around the same time, glad to get out alive.

Without Mikael, the young emperor tried to steer for himself, playing one great lord off against another. For a few years it worked. But every lord wanted a pliable emperor, and Tekle Haymanot was getting ideas. In April 1777 he was deposed. He died that September, aged about 23.

claims.text: Mikael Sehul was defeated by a coalition of lords in 1771.
claims.note: Recorded in the chronicles and by Bruce, who was still in the country; the standard histories agree.

claims.text: Tekle Haymanot II retired to a monastery after his fall.
claims.note: Later accounts say he withdrew to religious life before his death in 1777. The details are thin.

reigns.hook: The lords want an emperor who won't argue. They find a minor prince named Salomon and put him on the throne at Gondar.

reigns.tagline: Two years as a crowned figurehead
reigns.previously: Tekle Haymanot II gets ideas, and the lords throw him out.
paragraphs: Salomon II was what the lords wanted: royal enough to crown, too weak to matter. He sat in the old castles of Gondar while the real decisions were made in the camps of the regional lords. The city itself was shrinking, its palaces starting to crumble.

Even a figurehead could fall. In July 1779 the lords swapped him out and sent him up the prison mountain of Wehni. Within a year a rebel lord brought him down as a rival emperor, and lost. Salomon died in 1782. His successor was Tekle Giyorgis, another son of Yohannes II and brother of Tekle Haymanot II. That emperor would come and go so often that he set a record nobody wanted.

claims.text: Salomon II was a puppet with no real power.
claims.note: All the standard histories of the Era of the Princes describe the emperors of these years as figureheads for the great lords.

claims.text: The dates of Salomon II's reign follow the royal chronicle.
claims.note: Day dates come from the Royal Chronicle as summarised by later historians; other king lists give slightly different years.

reigns.hook: Salomon is out. In comes Tekle Giyorgis, son of old Yohannes II. He wants to be a real emperor, which in this era is a dangerous thing to want.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who would not stay deposed
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Rival royal; son of Yohannes II
reigns.reignEnded: Beaten by two rases at Afarwanat
reigns.previously: Salomon II, a figurehead for two years, is pushed aside.
paragraphs: Spare princes of the royal house lived under guard on Wehni, a sheer-sided mountain not far from Gondar. In July 1779 two lords, Kenfu Adam and his brother Hailu Adara, brought down Tekle Giyorgis, the youngest son of Yohannes II and brother of the deposed Tekle Haymanot II. He took the throne name Feqr Sagad. Unusually for this era, he wanted to actually rule.

He fell out with Kenfu within a year. Kenfu fetched the old ex-emperor Salomon II down from Wehni as a rival, but a loyal general beat him in May 1780. Tekle Giyorgis had the two brothers blinded instead of killed, which counted as mercy. He paid for a new church in Gondar, Debre Metmaq Maryam, and marched on Shewa to make its ruler kneel. At the Bashilo river his soldiers refused to go on.

In 1784 two rising lords turned on him: Ras Ali of the Yejju and Ras Haile Yosadiq of Gojjam. A Ras was a top-rank noble. They beat his army at Afarwanat and he fled to the mountain stronghold of Amba Sel. It was the first of six falls. Ethiopians later nicknamed him Fitsame Mengist, “the end of the kingdom”.

claims.text: Tekle Giyorgis was the last emperor of the era to rule on his own authority.
claims.note: The verdict of the historian Sven Rubenson, who tied it to his nickname. The royal chronicle shows him fighting hard, but always needing a lord's army.

claims.text: He spared the rebel brothers Kenfu Adam and Hailu Adara by blinding them.
claims.note: The royal chronicle for 1781 presents the blinding as an act of leniency in place of execution.

claims.text: He gave a crown to the monastery of Ura Kidane Mehret on Lake Tana.
claims.note: The attribution and the date of about 1780-85 come from the monastery museum's own label.

reigns.hook: Ras Ali and Ras Haile Yosadiq have their own man ready. They climb Wehni and bring down a grandson of Iyasu II.

reigns.tagline: A prince from the mountain, propped up by two rival lords
reigns.cameToPower: Made emperor by Ras Ali I
reigns.reignEnded: Dropped when Ras Ali switched sides
reigns.previously: Tekle Giyorgis I is beaten at Afarwanat and flees into exile.
paragraphs: Iyasu III was the son of a prince called Azequ and a grandson of Iyasu II. Ras Ali I and Ras Haile Yosadiq brought him down from Wehni in February 1784 and crowned him in Gondar. The Abuna, the bishop sent from Egypt, and the Ichege, head of the monks, watched the generals swear loyalty. Then the new emperor handed out titles, which was mostly what emperors were for now.

Ras Ali was the first of the Yejju regents, Oromo lords from the eastern edge of the highlands who would steer Gondar for most of the next seventy years. His alliance with Haile Yosadiq soon cracked, and the feuding lords kept Iyasu's four years busy. Before long Ali was bargaining with the very emperor they had thrown out.

In April 1788 Ali put Tekle Giyorgis back on the throne. Haile Yosadiq marched Iyasu into Gondar to fight for him, then left him behind when Ali's army came. Iyasu fled to Tigray, and later that year he was taken prisoner. Nobody knows when he died. The English traveller Henry Salt heard he was dead by 1810.

claims.text: Iyasu III died of smallpox soon after he was deposed.
claims.note: Budge says so, but the royal chronicle has him alive and captured after the battle of Madab in 1788. Salt only knew he was dead by 1810.

claims.text: Ras Ali I founded Debre Tabor, later the Yejju regents' capital.
claims.note: Abir credits him with it, but the royal chronicle never places Ali there and ties him to Filakit Gereger instead.

reigns.hook: Ras Ali has his old enemy back on the throne. But within two months Ali will be dead, and his brother Aligaz will have to fight his own family for the regency.

reigns.tagline: Back on the throne, and already on the run
reigns.reignEnded: Rival crowned while he was away
reigns.previously: Ras Ali I switches sides and drops Iyasu III.
paragraphs: Ras Ali I brought Tekle Giyorgis back from exile and crowned him again in April 1788. That spring Ali and the emperor beat an alliance of rival lords at the battle of Madab and captured their pretender, a prince called Baeda Maryam. For a moment Tekle Giyorgis looked safe.

Then Ali fell ill and died in June 1788. The royal chronicle blamed his drinking. His brother Aligaz took over as regent, but first he had to beat off his own relatives, who wanted the job too. Without a strong patron, Tekle Giyorgis was exposed.

In July 1789, while he was away fighting revolts, two Gondar officials climbed Wehni, brought down another prince, Hezqeyas, and made him emperor. Aligaz's men tried to trap the emperor's army near a village called Salam. Tekle Giyorgis slipped away and crossed the Blue Nile into Gojjam.

claims.text: Ras Ali I's fatal illness was caused by heavy drinking.
claims.note: This is the royal chronicler's opinion. No other account gives a cause.

claims.text: Aligaz's troops tried to encircle Tekle Giyorgis at Salam, and he escaped across the Blue Nile.
claims.note: Recorded in the royal chronicle, the main source for these years.

reigns.hook: Now there are two emperors. Hezqeyas sits in Gondar. Tekle Giyorgis holds court in Gojjam and hands out titles of his own.

reigns.cameToPower: Crowned while his rival was away
reigns.reignEnded: Beaten in battle, fled to Dengel Ber
reigns.previously: Tekle Giyorgis I is caught off guard and flees across the Blue Nile.
paragraphs: Hezqeyas was a son of Iyasu III, kept under guard on Wehni until two Gondar officials fetched him in July 1789. Tekle Giyorgis came back fast and Hezqeyas fled the city, then returned with fresh allies and drove his rival out again. The chronicler summed up the years that followed in a line: the kingdom was split in two.

His backer was the Yejju regent Ras Aligaz, busy at first beating his own relatives. Aligaz did lock up Tekle Giyorgis for a while at Emakina, which helped. But in 1792 Hezqeyas, the Abuna and the head of the monks held a council and swore they would not submit to the Galla, an old and now offensive name for the Oromo. That meant Aligaz. They lost the battle that followed.

Soon a lord freed Tekle Giyorgis from Emakina. After several battles Hezqeyas ran, and by January 1794 his rival was back. Hezqeyas lived for almost twenty more years. In 1802 his own son, the new emperor Egwale Seyon, met him on the road and escorted him into Gondar.

claims.text: Hezqeyas raided and laid waste the frontier with Sennar.
claims.note: Budge reports it. The royal chronicle tells a different story, mostly of flight and counter-flight around Gondar.

claims.text: His council vowed not to submit to the Galla, and lost the battle that followed.
claims.note: Recorded in the royal chronicle for 1792, translated by Weld Blundell.

claims.text: Fighting at the end of his reign set fire to part of Gondar's royal enclosure.
claims.note: The chronicle says men of Balambaras Asserat burned the Gan Takal while driving a rival lord out of the city.

reigns.hook: Tekle Giyorgis is back for a third time. To hold on, he needs Ras Aligaz, the very regent who kept him locked up.

reigns.reignEnded: Rival crowned while he was raiding
reigns.previously: Hezqeyas loses a string of battles and flees Gondar.
paragraphs: Tekle Giyorgis was back by January 1794. He went looking for friends and found doors shut. Dejazmach Gadlu, a lord north of Lake Tana, would not even receive him. A Dejazmach was a general, one rank below a Ras. The one man who would help was Ras Aligaz, camped with a large army at Chat Weha, the same regent who had lately kept him prisoner.

It worked for a while. With Aligaz's soldiers behind him he held Gondar for about fifteen months. But Gondar was shrinking. The great lords had carved up the emperor's lands and taxes, and the old palace compound, with its stone castles, was now a stage for ceremonies more than a seat of power.

In April 1795 he rode out to raid near Shawra. Behind his back a lord named Wolde Gabriel had another prince, Baeda Maryam, proclaimed emperor in Gondar, over the protests of the Abuna and the Ichege.

claims.text: Tekle Giyorgis was a great coward, a liar and a miser.
claims.note: So wrote Nathaniel Pearce, who knew him in old age. Pearce served his rival Ras Wolde Selassie, so the portrait may be unfair.

claims.text: A provincial lord refused even to receive the returning emperor.
claims.note: The royal chronicle records Dejazmach Gadlu's snub in 1794.

reigns.hook: Baeda Maryam II has a crown and almost no friends. In Lasta, a lord is already gathering an army with Oromo horsemen from Wollo.

reigns.tagline: Nine months as emperor, then decades of hoping
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Rival; maybe son of Salomon II
reigns.cameToPower: Proclaimed while the emperor was away
reigns.previously: Tekle Giyorgis I rides off raiding and loses Gondar behind his back.
paragraphs: Baeda Maryam II may have been a son of Salomon II, the puppet of the late 1770s. He was proclaimed in Gondar in April 1795 by Wolde Gabriel, who promptly made himself a Ras. The Abuna and the Ichege protested. Few other lords joined in, and his backer's men were soon brawling with a rival lord's retainers.

Late in 1795 Haile Wand Bewossen marched out of Lasta with Oromo horsemen from Wollo and beat Wolde Gabriel at Felaqit. Monks patched up a peace, Wolde Gabriel withdrew to a monastery, and Haile went to Gondar to invite Tekle Giyorgis back. Baeda Maryam's reign was over.

He never gave up. By 1802 he was a prisoner in Semien. In January 1813 he visited Ras Wolde Selassie, the great lord of Tigray, to ask for help winning back his throne. The Ras said no. Baeda Maryam II lived until 1833, outliving most of the men who had pushed him aside.

claims.text: Baeda Maryam II and Salomon III were the same man.
claims.note: Budge says some authorities thought so. Nathaniel Pearce, who met Baeda Maryam in 1813, was told he had reigned only once, for nine months.

claims.text: He was a son of Salomon II.
claims.note: Suggested in some king lists, but not firmly established.

reigns.tagline: The fourth crowning lasts just five months
reigns.cameToPower: Invited back by Haile Wand Bewossen
reigns.previously: Baeda Maryam II's only backer loses a battle at Felaqit.
paragraphs: Haile Wand Bewossen, the victor of Felaqit, summoned Tekle Giyorgis to Gondar in December 1795 and he was crowned for a fourth time. By now everyone knew the routine. Each new kingmaker needed a crowned emperor to sign off on his titles and lands, and Tekle Giyorgis was always available.

Real power sat far from Gondar. In Tigray, Ras Wolde Selassie ruled the north and would later host British visitors. The Yejju regent Aligaz held the centre. In May 1796 Wolde Selassie and his ally Ras Mare'ed backed a candidate of their own, Salomon III, and Tekle Giyorgis was out again after five months.

claims.text: Tekle Giyorgis was deposed and restored more often than any other Ethiopian emperor.
claims.note: The lists count his reigns as five or six. Only Sahle Dengel, with five turns in the 1830s to 1850s, comes close.

claims.text: Ras Wolde Selassie and Ras Mare'ed made Salomon III emperor.
claims.note: Both are named as his backers in the royal chronicle.

reigns.hook: Salomon III is crowned. He is a son of Tekle Haymanot II, so the two rivals are family, and they will spend the next year chasing each other around the highlands.

reigns.relationToPredecessor: Nephew; son of Tekle Haymanot II

reigns.reignEnded: Fled from a rebel to Axum
reigns.previously: Ras Wolde Selassie of Tigray wants an emperor of his own.
paragraphs: Salomon III was a son of Tekle Haymanot II, the teenage puppet of the 1770s. Ras Wolde Selassie of Tigray and Ras Mare'ed put him on the throne in May 1796. He spent the next year struggling with his uncle, the ever-returning Tekle Giyorgis, who had no intention of staying retired.

While the two were busy with each other, a rebel called Balambaras Asserat surrounded Gondar in May 1797. He was too weak to storm it, so he burned Tekle Giyorgis's property in the city instead. Salomon did not wait to see what came next. He fled to Axum, the ancient holy city of Tigray, and lived there under Wolde Selassie's protection. Back in Gondar, the rebels' side crowned a new emperor.

claims.text: Salomon III is the ex-emperor 'Solomon' whom Henry Salt listed as still alive in 1809-10.
claims.note: Salt names a living Solomon among the former emperors. This is the likeliest match, but he gives no detail.

claims.text: Asserat burned Tekle Giyorgis's property in Gondar.
claims.note: Recorded in the royal chronicle for 1797.

reigns.tagline: Crowned in a famine, a fugitive by winter
reigns.previously: Salomon III flees Gondar for Axum, ahead of a rebel lord.
paragraphs: Yonas came from a forgotten branch of the royal family descended from Fasilides, the builder of Gondar. He was proclaimed in August 1797 after the rebel Asserat drove Salomon III out. The timing was terrible. Famine swept the land, and the chronicler wrote that more people died than could be counted. Yonas's son Mafu and his wife Esther both died that autumn.

He had no army and no great lord behind him. The big men of the day, Ras Mare'ed, Hailu Eshte, Wolde Selassie of Tigray and Ras Guebra, asked Tekle Giyorgis to come back from exile in Waldebba, a district of monasteries north-west of Gondar. When Tekle Giyorgis was a day's march away, Yonas ran to the Abuna's palace and claimed sanctuary.
Later he was a prisoner in Lasta, then an exile in Gojjam. He died in May 1813 so poor, Nathaniel Pearce wrote, that there was not even money for a coffin.

claims.text: Yonas was a grandson of Fasilides.
claims.note: Some lists call him a son of Letezum and grandson of Fasilides, who died in 1667. A gap of 130 years makes a later descendant far more likely.

claims.text: He died without enough money to buy a coffin.
claims.note: Reported by Nathaniel Pearce, who was living in Ethiopia at the time.

reigns.hook: Tekle Giyorgis rides into Gondar for the fifth time. First job: deal with the ex-emperor hiding in the Abuna's palace before a rebel grabs him.

reigns.tagline: Fifth crowning, and his longest stay since 1784
reigns.previously: Yonas hides in the Abuna's palace as Tekle Giyorgis returns.
paragraphs: In January 1798 the great lords brought Tekle Giyorgis back from Waldebba and crowned him a fifth time. One of his first problems was Yonas, still hiding in sanctuary. When a rebel named Waheldu, Asserat's brother, tried to grab Yonas as his own puppet, Tekle Giyorgis offered a pardon and moved Yonas and his brother into the royal enclosure, where he could keep an eye on them.

This was the emperor's job now. He had a palace, a title and a church that blessed whoever wore the crown. He had no treasury worth the name, no army of his own and few provinces paying him tax. Lords made emperors so that their own grabs looked lawful.

Salomon III had not gone away. He had been living with Tekle Giyorgis as a guest, then slipped off to Gondar while the emperor was campaigning. In May 1799 Ras Mare'ed and Ras Guebra set Salomon on the throne again, and Tekle Giyorgis was out for the fifth time.

claims.text: Tekle Giyorgis pardoned Yonas to stop rebels using him.
claims.note: The royal chronicle says he had Yonas and his brother Goshu live with him in friendship in the royal enclosure.

claims.text: Salomon III escaped from Tekle Giyorgis's own camp to reclaim the throne.
claims.note: From the royal chronicle as summarised by modern writers, who disagree over whether this happened in 1797 or 1799.

reigns.hook: Salomon III is back on the throne. But the lords who restored him have enemies, and those enemies are marching on Gondar.

reigns.tagline: Two months back on the throne, then chains
reigns.cameToPower: Restored by Ras Mare'ed and Ras Guebra
reigns.reignEnded: Deposed and chained after a battle
reigns.previously: Salomon III slips away to Gondar and is crowned once more.
paragraphs: Salomon III's second reign lasted about two months. Ras Mare'ed and Ras Guebra, the lords who had brought him back, had powerful enemies, and those enemies marched on Gondar.

In the battle that followed, that July, Mare'ed was killed. His side lost, and Salomon lost with it. Two of the winners, Dejazmach Gugsa and Dejazmach Alula of the Yejju ruling family, put him in chains and within days crowned a new emperor, Demetros. In 1802 Salomon was still a prisoner, now in Tigray.
Gugsa was the one to watch. Within a few years he would be Ras Gugsa, regent of the centre and the strongest Yejju lord of them all.

claims.text: A rival lord named Wolde Gabriel was also killed in the battle.
claims.note: Some summaries of the royal chronicle say so, but several lords of that name appear in these years, and the one who crowned Baeda Maryam II withdrew to a monastery in 1795. Who fell here is unclear.

claims.text: Gugsa, who chained Salomon, became regent and held power until 1825.
claims.note: Abir and the royal chronicle agree that Ras Gugsa of Yejju dominated Gondar from about 1803 until his death in 1825.

reigns.hook: Salomon is in chains. The Yejju lords have their new emperor, Demetros, whose royal blood plenty of people doubt.
