reigns.tagline: A prince of doubtful blood, crowned by the Yejju brothers
reigns.relationToPredecessor: None known; son of one Arqedewos
reigns.previously: Salomon III's second turn ends after two months, in chains.
paragraphs: Demetros was the son of a man called Arqedewos, and the royal blood that was meant to come with that was hard to prove. It hardly mattered. In July 1799 two brothers from Yejju, Dejazmach Gugsa and Alula, put Salomon III in chains and sat Demetros on the throne in Gondar. (A dejazmach was a top-rank general, one step below a ras.)

He paid them back fast. Within days he made Gugsa lord of Begemder, the rich province east of Lake Tana, and gave Alula a court title too. That was the real job of an emperor now: handing out titles to the men who had made him. Gugsa would go on to be the strongest man in central Ethiopia for a quarter of a century.

In March 1800 old Tekle Giyorgis marched back into Gondar, backed by Ras Wolde Selassie, the great lord of Tigray. He made a point of not moving into the palace. Everyone understood that Demetros was out anyway.

claims.text: Demetros was of the royal line.
claims.note: The chronicle names his father as Arqedewos; modern king lists class him as non-dynastic or of doubtful descent.

claims.text: He may be the ex-emperor 'Adimo' whom Henry Salt heard about in Tigray.
claims.note: Salt mentions an Adimo already dead by his 1809–10 visit; matching him to Demetros is a modern guess.

reigns.hook: Tekle Giyorgis is back on the throne for the sixth time. He is about fifty, and the lords who keep throwing him out keep needing him. Can he hold on this time?

reigns.tagline: Sixth time on the throne, and the last
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Yohannes II; ousted Demetros
reigns.previously: Tekle Giyorgis marches back into Gondar. Demetros is out.
paragraphs: No one in Ethiopian history came back as often as Tekle Giyorgis. This was his sixth reign, and it lasted only a few months. His backer was Ras Wolde Selassie of Tigray, the strongest lord in the north, who liked having an emperor in Gondar he could deal with.

But Tigray was a long way off, and Gondar belonged to whoever had troops nearby. In June 1800, while Tekle Giyorgis was out fighting in the provinces, his enemies hauled Demetros back to the palace and crowned him again. The chronicle says Demetros did not even want it.

Tekle Giyorgis never reigned again, though he never stopped hoping. He lived another seventeen years. The Englishman Nathaniel Pearce, who knew him in his sixties, found him tall, vain about his long plaited hair, stingy and not to be trusted. He died on 12 December 1817.

claims.text: Ras Wolde Selassie was still thinking of restoring him in 1813.
claims.note: Pearce says so, adding that the Ras wanted to wait for a new bishop from Egypt first. Nothing came of it.

claims.text: Ethiopian tradition calls him Fitsame Mengist, 'the end of the government'.
claims.note: Sven Rubenson reports the nickname; it is also translated 'the end of the kingdom'.

reigns.hook: Demetros is back on a throne he never asked for. Who put him there, and how long will they want him?

reigns.tagline: Crowned again, against his will
reigns.previously: Tekle Giyorgis is away at war. Demetros is hauled back to the palace.
paragraphs: The chronicle tells Demetros's second reign almost as a farce. He was dragged to the palace and crowned while Tekle Giyorgis was off campaigning, with no say in the matter. The chronicler, watching kings come and go, was disgusted. He wrote a prayer of grief for 'those revered kings', asking God to restore the crown as He had once restored it from the Zagwe to the house of David.

This time Demetros lasted about a year. Then, in June 1801, the two great lords of the day, Ras Wolde Selassie of Tigray and Gugsa of Yejju, agreed that the merry-go-round had to stop. They chose a new emperor and both backed him. Demetros died in 1802 and was buried at Ba'ata.

claims.text: Demetros was crowned the second time against his will.
claims.note: So says the Royal Chronicle; no other account of the scene survives.

claims.text: The court chronicler wrote a lament over how often emperors were made and unmade.
claims.note: The passage is in the Royal Chronicle as translated by H. Weld Blundell in 1922.

reigns.hook: The lords of Tigray and Yejju have picked a son of the old emperor Hezqeyas. He will reign for seventeen years, longer than anyone else in this era, and do almost nothing.

reigns.tagline: Seventeen years on the throne by being harmless
reigns.cameToPower: Chosen by Gugsa and Wolde Selassie
reigns.previously: Demetros's year is up. The great lords agree on a new emperor.
paragraphs: Egwale Seyon, throne name Newaya Sagad, was a son of Hezqeyas, emperor in the 1790s. Ras Wolde Selassie of Tigray and Gugsa of Yejju chose him to end the chaos, and Gugsa tied him closer by marrying him to his own sister, Walatta Iyasus. They had five children.

He was safe because he was powerless. After one early trip out with Gugsa he never left Gondar again. The chronicler grumbled that nothing happened, good or bad, because a Galla held the real power. (Galla is an old, now offensive name for the Oromo; Gugsa was an Oromo lord.) Outside, Gugsa, Ras Zewde of Gojjam and Wolde Selassie fought for years.

The British envoy Henry Salt heard that the emperor lived neglected in Gondar with a few servants and too little money to keep up his dignity. Royalty, Salt wrote, was almost eclipsed. Egwale Seyon's name lives on at Debre Berhan Selassie, Gondar's famous painted church, which he supported. He died in office on 12 June 1818.

claims.text: In 1809 Ras Zewde of Gojjam tried to swap him for Tekle Giyorgis, but Zewde's army refused to fight Gugsa.
claims.note: The Royal Chronicle dates the stand-off to 24 February 1809; Zewde escaped on foot.

claims.text: Egwale Seyon is shown in the paintings of Debre Berhan Selassie.
claims.note: His patronage is argued mainly from royal figures in the church's murals; the identifications are not certain.

claims.text: He was sickly all his life.
claims.note: Nathaniel Pearce, living in Ethiopia at the time, said so after the emperor's death.

reigns.hook: Egwale Seyon is dead. Ras Gugsa needs another quiet emperor, and he does not like the dead man's nephews. His choice is a monk.

reigns.tagline: The monk Ras Gugsa preferred to the nephews
reigns.previously: Egwale Seyon dies in office after seventeen quiet years.
paragraphs: Iyoas II was another son of Hezqeyas, and before he was emperor he lived as a monk in Waldebba, a remote district famous for its hermits. Nathaniel Pearce, an English sailor who had settled in Ethiopia, heard that Ras Gugsa and Kenyazmach Akli Meru looked at Egwale Seyon's nephews, Zerobabel and Merrit, and judged them bad characters. The monk got the crown instead.

The Royal Chronicle barely notices him. It records the day he was raised up and the year he died, and very little in between. The missionary Samuel Gobat summed him up a few years later: Gugsa was his firm support, or rather his superior. Iyoas died on 3 June 1821, still emperor, and Gondar was left without one for a while.

claims.text: Gugsa passed over Egwale Seyon's nephews because of their bad characters.
claims.note: Only Pearce says so, and he heard it at second hand in Tigray.

claims.text: Iyoas II had been a monk in Waldebba before he was crowned.
claims.note: Reported by Pearce; it fits the habit of keeping spare princes in religious life.

reigns.hook: Iyoas is dead and the regent wants another man of prayer. He finds an old monk, said to be Iyoas's brother, who is already in his seventies.

reigns.previously: Iyoas II dies in office. The regent goes looking for another monk.
paragraphs: Gigar had spent many years as a monk when the call came in 1821. He was about 76. Like the two emperors before him, he was there to agree to whatever the Yejju regents wanted, first Ras Gugsa and, after Gugsa died in 1825, his son Ras Yimam.

His family tree was murky. Samuel Gobat was told he was a brother of Iyoas II; other lists make him a son of Iyasu II. Nobody at court seems to have cared. The crown no longer needed a strong claim, only a quiet wearer.

In April 1826 Dejazmach Haile Maryam, governor of the mountain province of Semien, came down on Gondar with an emperor of his own. Ras Yimam was away at war in Gojjam, and for a few days Gigar was out.

claims.text: Gigar was Iyoas II's brother.
claims.note: Gobat says so; modern king lists make him possibly a son of Iyasu II instead. Iyoas II was a son of Hezqeyas.

claims.text: He was born around 1745.
claims.note: Worked back from the age Gobat was given in 1830, which Gobat himself doubted.

reigns.hook: Haile Maryam of Semien has crowned his own man, a Baeda Maryam. But the Yejju regent is already turning his army round.

reigns.cameToPower: Put up by Haile Maryam of Semien
reigns.previously: Haile Maryam of Semien marches on Gondar. Gigar is pushed aside.
paragraphs: Baeda Maryam III was the figurehead of Dejazmach Haile Maryam, governor of Semien. The Royal Chronicle says Haile Maryam marched south and held Mount Manta for fifteen days to make him emperor. Little is known of his family, and modern lists do not count him as royal.

Ras Yimam of Yejju broke off his campaign in Gojjam and raced back. Finding Haile Maryam holding the fords of the Abay, the Blue Nile, he swung round the west side of Lake Tana to reach him. Haile Maryam fell back, fought Yimam and his brother Marye for three days and escaped. His emperor was finished, and Gigar was back.
Baeda Maryam did not vanish. In June 1831 Samuel Gobat met him with his wife and children at Adigrat in Tigray, living on as a former emperor.

claims.text: Baeda Maryam III was the same man as Baeda Maryam II, emperor for a few months in 1795.
claims.note: Argued by the historian Elisabeth-Dorothea Hecht; the king lists count two people.

claims.text: His reign lasted only days.
claims.note: The Royal Chronicle and later lists put the whole episode in April 1826.

reigns.hook: Gigar is back, now past eighty. Soon a Swiss missionary will call on him with a gift the old emperor does not want.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who wanted silk, not Gospels
reigns.previously: Baeda Maryam III's backers retreat. His reign lasts a few days.
paragraphs: The Yejju lords put Gigar back within days. In 1830 the Swiss missionary Samuel Gobat reached Gondar and met him. Gigar was said to be 86, though Gobat thought he looked sixty-five or seventy, and decided the monk's cowl had suited him better than the crown.

He lived in one curtained room of a small round house beside the old palace. Proudly he showed Gobat the crumbling halls and asked if he had ever seen anything so grand. Gobat said there were buildings at home to match it. Gigar was amazed that anyone alive could still build like that.

Gobat gave him printed Gospels in Amharic. A few days later Gigar sent them back: he had plenty of books, he said, and would much rather have some cloth or a piece of silk. He lived on whatever the lords chose to send. In June 1830 they replaced him.

claims.text: Gigar sent back Gobat's Gospels and asked for cloth or silk instead.
claims.note: Told by Gobat himself in the journal of his years in Abyssinia.

claims.text: He was 86 when Gobat met him.
claims.note: That was the age Gobat was given; he thought Gigar looked far younger. The lists give a birth year of about 1745.

reigns.hook: The old monk is out. The new emperor is Iyasu IV, a son of Salomon III, and he soon finds that sitting quietly in Gondar is not for him.

reigns.tagline: The puppet emperor who went out raiding
reigns.cameToPower: Set up by the Yejju regents
reigns.previously: Old Gigar is deposed. A son of Salomon III gets the crown.
paragraphs: Iyasu IV was a son of Salomon III, one of the short-lived emperors of the 1790s. The Yejju regents crowned him in June 1830. In February 1831 the regent Ras Marye was killed fighting Sabagadis of Tigray at Debre Abbay, and soon a young member of the family, Ras Ali II, held the regency.

Iyasu was meant to stay in Gondar and do nothing. Instead he rode about the countryside and led raids, as if he were a warlord himself. When Ras Ali heard about it, he threw the emperor out, in March 1832.

claims.text: Old Gigar brought him down by falsely accusing him of inviting a rival lord to overthrow Ras Ali.
claims.note: Samuel Gobat wrote this in his journal; it is hearsay from Gondar.

claims.text: Iyasu was removed because he went raiding on his own account.
claims.note: The usual explanation in the lists and later histories; Gobat's journal blames Gigar's plotting instead.

reigns.hook: Ras Ali II needs a new emperor. He picks Gebre Krestos, whose family claimed to descend from a younger son of Fasilides, two centuries back.

paragraphs: Gebre Krestos was the son of Gebre Mesay, and his family said they came down from a younger son of Fasilides, the emperor who built Gondar's first castle. In March 1832 the Yejju regent Ras Ali II set him on the throne.

It did not last. Within weeks Ali changed his mind and put Gebre Krestos's brother Sahle Dengel in his place. Gebre Krestos was sent to Mitraha, an island in Lake Tana, a handy spot for keeping a spare emperor out of the way.

claims.note: The chronicle tradition and later lists repeat the family's claim; there is no way to check it.

claims.text: He reigned two short turns in 1832, less than three months in all.
claims.note: The Royal Chronicle and the lists agree on 1832; exact days differ between sources.

reigns.previously: Ras Ali II sends Gebre Krestos to an island and crowns his brother.
paragraphs: Sahle Dengel was born in 1778, so he was in his fifties when Ras Ali II put him in his brother's place in the spring of 1832. He was a cultivated man, and he would turn out to be the great survivor of the era, taking the throne five separate times.

This first turn was short. The Ethiopian church was split by long, bitter arguments over doctrine, and the clergy of Azazo, near Gondar, disliked where Sahle Dengel stood. They talked Ras Ali into dropping him. Sahle Dengel was sent away to Zengaj, and Ali fetched Gebre Krestos back from his island.

claims.text: The clergy of Azazo had him removed over his religious beliefs.
claims.note: Reported only in the chronicle tradition, which does not spell out exactly which teaching offended them.

claims.text: He reigned five separate times between 1832 and 1855.
claims.note: The king lists count five turns, though several boundaries are known only to the year.

reigns.previously: The clergy turn on Sahle Dengel. He is sent away to Zengaj.
paragraphs: The priests had won, and Gebre Krestos came back from Mitraha to the throne. He did not last long. On 8 June 1832 he was dead. He was buried at the church of Tekle Haymanot at Adababay in Gondar.

For a few months there was no emperor at all, and nobody seems to have missed one. Ras Ali carried on running things, as he had all along. Then Sahle Dengel went to meet him at a village called Tagur and talked his way back to the crown, in October 1832.

claims.text: Gebre Krestos was poisoned.
claims.note: E. A. Wallis Budge reports that some authorities thought so; no contemporary evidence is cited.

claims.text: The throne stood empty for months after his death.
claims.note: The king lists show a gap from June to October 1832.

reigns.hook: Sahle Dengel has charmed Ras Ali into giving him the crown back. This time he will keep it for eight years, and early on a self-proclaimed prophet-king will lose his head over it.

reigns.cameToPower: Talked Ras Ali into restoring him
reigns.previously: Gebre Krestos dies in office. The throne in Gondar is empty again.
paragraphs: Sahle Dengel had already been emperor once in 1832, for a few weeks, until the clergy of Azezo complained about his religious views and the regent had him packed off. When Gebre Krestos died that June, Sahle Dengel went to see the regent, Ras Ali II, in person and talked his way back. By October he was King of Kings again, at about 54.

Ras Ali was barely a teenager, and his mother, Menen Liben Amede, ran much of the regency from the Yejju base at Debre Tabor. The emperor in Gondar had a title, a seal and a crumbling palace. The German naturalist Eduard Rüppell, there in 1833, reckoned his income was about that of a comfortably-off local farmer. In 1838 Ali's own troops sacked Gondar.

Sahle Dengel still used his title. In 1839 he was one of the signers of a letter, carried to London by the French traveller Antoine d'Abbadie, asking Queen Victoria to rein in Egyptian troops raiding the western border. Then Menen decided she wanted a royal of her own on the throne: her husband.

claims.text: In 1832 Sahle Dengel cut off the head of a rival claimant, Egwale Anbesa, and hung it in a tree.
claims.note: Told in the Royal Chronicle, the only account. The chronicle was written for the winning side.

claims.text: The clergy of Azezo got him removed in 1832 over his religious views.
claims.note: The chronicle reports it without saying which views offended. The church was split by bitter quarrels over doctrine at the time.

claims.text: Rüppell found the emperor barely richer than an ordinary well-off Ethiopian.
claims.note: Rüppell says so in the account of his 1833 visit to Gondar.

reigns.hook: Empress Menen has put her own husband on the throne. Yohannes III is the son of a famous emperor and, it turns out, has a dangerous taste in friends.

reigns.tagline: The empress's husband, crowned by his wife
reigns.cameToPower: Put in by his wife, Empress Menen
reigns.reignEnded: Deposed by his stepson Ras Ali
reigns.previously: Empress Menen deposes Sahle Dengel and crowns her own husband.
paragraphs: Yohannes was a son of Tekle Giyorgis I, the emperor who had been thrown out and brought back half a dozen times. His royal blood was one asset. His wife was the other. Menen Liben Amede, mother of the regent Ras Ali II, had married him, and in October 1839 she won the fight for Gojjam at Chenti Ber. In August 1840 she dropped Sahle Dengel and crowned her husband.

Now Menen was Itege, empress, as well as the regent's mother. But Yohannes backed the wrong man. Ras Ali's great rival was Dejazmach Wube Haile Maryam, lord of Semien and Tigray, and Yohannes showed him favour. Ali would not stand for it. In October 1841 he threw out his stepfather and brought Sahle Dengel back.

claims.text: Yohannes lost the throne for siding with Ras Ali's rival Wube.
claims.note: This is the reason the standard histories give, though the inner politics of the Yejju court are poorly recorded.

claims.text: Yohannes was a drunk and a glutton, tolerated only for his royal blood.
claims.note: That is E. A. Wallis Budge's verdict (1928), written long afterwards with little evidence. Other historians are kinder.

reigns.hook: Out goes the empress's husband and back comes old Sahle Dengel. Within months Ras Ali has to fight for his life against Wube at Debre Tabor.

reigns.tagline: Back on the throne while the warlords fought it out
reigns.previously: Ras Ali removes Yohannes for befriending his rival Wube.
paragraphs: Sahle Dengel's third reign opened with a war. In February 1842 Wube of Semien and his allies marched on Ras Ali's base at Debre Tabor. The battle went badly for Ali, who fled, but by the end of the day Wube was somehow a prisoner. Ali came out of it stronger than ever.

In Gondar, Sahle Dengel went on being emperor in name. He kept writing letters under his seal, and visitors found a friendly, easygoing old man. The French traveller Arnauld d'Abbadie described him with snow-white hair, a smooth beardless face and a cheerful, earthy manner, sitting on a worn inlaid bed with a carpet too small for the floor.
None of this decided anything. Whoever held Gondar could crown an emperor, and around 1845 somebody decided to swap him again.

claims.text: At Debre Tabor in 1842 Wube won the battle, then was captured while his men celebrated.
claims.note: Told in several 19th-century accounts. They differ on exactly how Wube was taken.

claims.text: Arnauld d'Abbadie met Sahle Dengel and described him in detail.
claims.note: In his book on twelve years in Ethiopia, published in 1868.

reigns.hook: Around 1845 the throne changes hands again, for a moment. Yohannes III is back, and nobody is quite sure why.

reigns.tagline: A second reign so short the records barely notice it
reigns.previously: Around 1845 Sahle Dengel is pushed aside once more.
paragraphs: Yohannes III's second reign is one of the thinnest entries in Ethiopian history. The king lists agree that it happened around 1845 and that it was short. They say nothing about why he was put back on the throne, or why he was taken off it again.

That tells you a lot about the time. The story that mattered was out west, in Qwara near the Sudan border. A young chief there called Kassa Hailu had turned outlaw and was building a following of tough, loyal fighters. He came from a minor noble family that had fallen on hard times, and his enemies never let him forget it.

claims.text: Kassa's enemies sneered that his mother sold kosso, a medicine for tapeworm, in the market.
claims.note: A jibe from his rivals. His family did lose its standing after his father died, but the market story is unproven.

claims.text: Yohannes III had a brief second reign around 1845.
claims.note: It appears in the regnal lists, but no exact dates survive.

reigns.hook: Sahle Dengel is back again. And on the shores of Lake Tana, Kassa Hailu is about to embarrass the most powerful woman in Ethiopia.

reigns.tagline: The old emperor watches an outlaw capture the empress
reigns.previously: Yohannes III's brief second turn ends. Sahle Dengel is back.
paragraphs: Sahle Dengel, now in his late sixties, was back in Gondar's palace. Out west Kassa Hailu was growing stronger. In October 1846 he beat two detachments of Empress Menen's army. On 18 June 1847, near Lake Tana, he beat Menen herself and took both her and her husband Yohannes prisoner.

Ras Ali had to bargain for his mother. He made Kassa a dejazmach, a high-ranking lord, with lands north of Lake Tana. Kassa married Ali's daughter Tewabech around 1848. That year he also attacked an Egyptian fort at Dabarki on the Sudan border and was beaten by disciplined troops with modern guns.

Sahle Dengel, meanwhile, wrote letters. In April 1848 he sent a packet to Samuel Gobat, the Anglican bishop in Jerusalem, asking for help in getting the Ethiopian monks' monastery of Dar es-Sultan back. Around 1850 he was pushed aside yet again.

claims.text: Kassa traded the captive Empress Menen back to her son for a title and lands.
claims.note: Reported at the time and accepted by historians such as Sven Rubenson.

claims.text: Kassa loved Tewabech and stayed faithful to her until her death in 1858.
claims.note: So say his admirers and early biographers. It is hard to test.

claims.text: The defeat at Dabarki taught Kassa to value modern firearms.
claims.note: A common reading by historians of his later obsession with guns; Kassa left no account of it himself.

reigns.hook: Around 1850 Yohannes III somehow gets the crown back for a third and final time. He has a new interest: the Catholic missionaries in the north.

reigns.tagline: The puppet emperor who turned Catholic
reigns.previously: Sahle Dengel is pushed aside around 1850. Yohannes III is back.
paragraphs: Nobody recorded how Yohannes III got back on the throne around 1850. Even the old histories admit they don't know. The reign lasted about a year, and then Sahle Dengel was restored. Yohannes kept up his claim, and for a while different corners of the broken country named different emperors.

He had found new friends. Catholic missionaries under the Italian priest Justin de Jacobis were working in the north, and Yohannes became a Catholic in 1851. When Kassa was crowned he accepted it without a fight. Later he went back to the Orthodox church and lived at Tewodros's court, a harmless leftover of the old order. He died around 1873.

claims.text: Yohannes III became a Catholic in 1851.
claims.note: Donald Crummey's study of the missions says so. He later returned to the Orthodox church.

claims.text: He only accepted Tewodros on condition that he never had to live with Menen again.
claims.note: A story in some later accounts. No source from the time confirms it.

claims.text: In 1869 he wrote to Napoleon III asking for money.
claims.note: A letter from him dated 11 June 1869 survives.

reigns.hook: Sahle Dengel is crowned for the fifth time, aged over seventy. Out west, Kassa Hailu has broken with Ras Ali and is coming for the lords one by one.

reigns.tagline: The last puppet of the Era of the Princes
reigns.previously: Yohannes III is pushed off the throne for the last time.
paragraphs: Sahle Dengel's fifth reign was his last, and the old system's too. Kassa Hailu had fallen out with Ras Ali. In November 1852 he beat and killed Goshu Zewde of Gojjam at Gur Amba. In 1853 he crushed another of Ali's lords and then Ali himself, at Ayshal on 29 June. Ali fled to his kinsmen in Wollo and never mattered again.

That left Wube of Semien and Tigray. On 9 February 1855 Kassa beat him at Deresge. Two days later, in the church there, the bishop Abuna Salama crowned Kassa King of Kings. He took the name Tewodros, out of an old prophecy about a just king. Sahle Dengel, about 77, simply stopped being emperor, and died that same year.
The Era of the Princes was over. Gondar would never again be the real seat of power.

claims.text: Kassa chose the name Tewodros to claim a prophecy of a king who would end Ethiopia's misery.
claims.note: The prophecy is real and well known; how far Kassa planned his career around it is debated.

claims.text: Ras Ali II lived on in obscurity in Wollo after Ayshal.
claims.note: The sources lose track of him. A death around 1866 is often given.

reigns.hook: Kassa Hailu is now Tewodros II, King of Kings, a self-made emperor with big dreams of a united, modern Ethiopia, and a temper to match.

reigns.tagline: The outsider who reunited Ethiopia and died at Magdala
reigns.relationToPredecessor: No royal kin; a border chief
reigns.cameToPower: Beat the princes one by one
reigns.previously: Kassa Hailu beats the princes. Puppet emperor Sahle Dengel is out.
paragraphs: Kassa Hailu came from Qwara, a rough border land, and his enemies sneered at his humble birth. He crushed the great lords anyway, and on 11 February 1855 he was crowned. He took the name Tewodros from an old prophecy of a king who would come to restore Ethiopia.

He meant it. He wanted one strong state, a real army and an end to the princes' private wars. He set European missionaries at Gafat to casting cannon, including a huge mortar he called Sebastopol. But rebellions kept flaring, and his rule grew more violent each year.

When Queen Victoria failed to answer his letter, he jailed the British consul, Charles Cameron, and other Europeans. Britain sent an army under Robert Napier. On 13 April 1868 the British stormed his mountain fortress of Magdala. Tewodros shot himself rather than be taken.

claims.text: The pistol he killed himself with was a gift from Queen Victoria.
claims.note: Told by members of the British expedition soon after. The story is famous but hard to prove.

claims.text: He kept European captives because his letter to Queen Victoria went unanswered.
claims.note: The letter was shelved at the Foreign Office; Rassam's and Markham's accounts and later historians agree this sparked the crisis.

claims.text: His young son Alemayehu was taken to England and died there in 1879.
claims.note: Buried at St George's Chapel, Windsor. Ethiopia has asked for his remains back.

reigns.hook: Tewodros is dead and the British are marching home. Who will be King of Kings now? The lord of Lasta moves first.

reigns.tagline: The lord of Lasta who grabbed the crown and lost it
reigns.previously: Tewodros shoots himself as the British storm Magdala.
paragraphs: Wagshum Gobeze was the hereditary lord of Lasta, the mountain country of Lalibela's rock churches. His father's line claimed descent from the old Zagwe kings. When Tewodros died, Gobeze moved fast and in August 1868 he was proclaimed emperor, taking the name Tekle Giyorgis.

Not everyone agreed. In Shewa, Menelik was building his own power. In Tigray, Dejazmach Kassa Mercha refused to bow. Kassa had helped the British on their march to Magdala, and they paid him with guns and ammunition as they left.
In July 1871 the two armies met at Assam, near Adwa. Kassa's better-armed men won, and the emperor was taken prisoner. He died in captivity a couple of years later.

claims.text: British guns given to Kassa decided the battle of Assam.
claims.note: Napier did leave Kassa artillery and muskets. How much they mattered, compared with Kassa's skill and numbers, is debated.

claims.text: His family descended from the Zagwe kings.
claims.note: The Wagshum lords of Lasta claimed it. It can't be traced back that far.

reigns.hook: Kassa of Tigray holds the emperor in chains. Now he wants a crown of his own, and he means to take it in the holiest city in the land.

reigns.tagline: The warrior emperor who fought everyone and fell to a sniper
reigns.cameToPower: Won at Assam, crowned at Aksum
reigns.previously: Kassa of Tigray beats Tekle Giyorgis at Assam and takes him prisoner.
paragraphs: Kassa Mercha was crowned on 21 January 1872 at Aksum, the ancient holy city, as Yohannes IV. He was a fierce churchman and a hard fighter, and he needed to be. Egypt was pushing up from the coast. Yohannes smashed its armies at Gundet in 1875 and Gura in 1876.

Then came Italy, which took over the port of Massawa in 1885. Yohannes's great general Ras Alula wiped out an Italian column at Dogali in 1887. At home Yohannes let Menelik of Shewa keep his title of Negus, or king, in return for loyalty. Neither man fully trusted the other.

In the west, the Mahdist state of Sudan raided deep into Ethiopia. In March 1889 Yohannes attacked them at Metemma. His army was winning when he was hit by a bullet. He died of the wound, and his army fell apart.

claims.text: The Mahdists cut off his head and sent it to Omdurman.
claims.note: Both Sudanese and Ethiopian accounts say his body was seized and the head taken to the Khalifa as a trophy.

claims.text: On his deathbed he named his son Mengesha as heir.
claims.note: Mengesha's supporters said so. Menelik ignored it, and the claim came too late to matter.

reigns.hook: The emperor is dead on the Sudan border and Tigray is reeling. In Shewa, Menelik doesn't wait. He declares himself King of Kings.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who beat Italy and built Addis Ababa
reigns.cameToPower: Claimed the crown when Yohannes fell
reigns.previously: Yohannes IV is killed fighting the Mahdists at Metemma.
paragraphs: As a boy, Menelik was Tewodros's prisoner at Magdala. He escaped in 1865 and made himself King of Shewa. With his clever wife, Empress Taytu, he founded a new capital in 1886 at Addis Ababa, which means new flower. When Yohannes died, he took the imperial crown.

In 1889 he signed the Treaty of Wuchale with Italy. Article 17 said in Amharic that he could use Italy for foreign affairs. The Italian text said he must, which made Ethiopia a protectorate. Menelik refused, and Italy invaded. On 1 March 1896, at Adwa, his armies crushed the Italians. Europe had to accept that Ethiopia was free.

He also conquered vast lands to the south and roughly doubled the empire. A railway from French Djibouti crept inland. From 1906 a run of strokes slowly left him helpless, and in 1909 he named his young grandson Lij Iyasu as heir.

claims.text: He ordered electric chairs from America and used one as a throne.
claims.note: A popular story with no good evidence. There was no power supply to run one anyway.

claims.text: When ill, he ate pages torn from the Bible as medicine.
claims.note: Told by Europeans at court. It fits a real belief in holy books as cures, but the details can't be checked.

claims.text: Adwa was the decisive defeat of a European colonial army by an African state.
claims.note: Italy signed the Treaty of Addis Ababa in October 1896, recognising Ethiopian independence.

reigns.hook: Menelik is gone. The throne passes to a restless teenage grandson whose father was born a Muslim, and the old Shewan lords are already worried.

reigns.tagline: The teenage heir who was never crowned
reigns.cameToPower: Named heir by his dying grandfather
reigns.reignEnded: Deposed by the nobles and church
reigns.previously: Menelik II dies after years of strokes. His grandson takes charge.
paragraphs: Lij Iyasu was Menelik's grandson through his daughter Shewaregga. "Lij" simply marks a young noble, and he never got a grander title because he was never crowned. His father was Ras Mikael of Wollo, a great lord born a Muslim who had turned Christian under Yohannes IV. Menelik's death was kept quiet, so Iyasu ran the empire as a teenager while the old Shewan lords watched him closely.

He was restless and spent little time in Addis Ababa, roaming the east and the lowlands. He courted Muslim chiefs and married into their families, and during the First World War he leaned towards the Ottomans and Germany, which alarmed Britain, France and Italy. In September 1916 the Shewan nobles, backed by the church, declared him deposed for abandoning the faith.

His father marched on the capital and was crushed at Segale on 27 October 1916. Iyasu stayed on the run for years until he was caught in 1921, and he spent the rest of his life a prisoner. His death was announced in November 1935, just as Italy invaded.

claims.text: Iyasu secretly converted to Islam.
claims.note: His enemies said so and circulated photographs of him in Muslim dress; historians suspect at least some were faked, and his Muslim alliances were also plain politics.

claims.text: Iyasu was murdered in captivity in 1935.
claims.note: Some accounts blame Haile Selassie's government as Italy invaded; others say he died naturally. How he died and where he lies are still unknown.

claims.text: Menelik's death was kept secret for nearly three years.
claims.note: The Council of State and the church only announced it officially in September 1916, on the same day they deposed Iyasu.

reigns.hook: With Iyasu gone, the nobles need someone safe on the throne. They pick Menelik's daughter Zewditu, and make her ambitious cousin Ras Tafari the heir.

reigns.relationToPredecessor: Daughter of Menelik II; Iyasu's aunt
reigns.cameToPower: Put on the throne by the nobles
reigns.reignEnded: Died two days after her husband
reigns.previously: The nobles depose Lij Iyasu, accused of turning Muslim.
paragraphs: Zewditu was Menelik's daughter, and when the nobles threw out Lij Iyasu they made her the first woman to reign over Ethiopia in her own right. She was crowned in February 1917. Devout and conservative, she spent long hours in prayer. The deal came with a catch: her cousin Ras Tafari Makonnen was named regent and heir, and in practice he ran the government. Everyone knew it.

Tafari was young, clever and in a hurry. He took Ethiopia into the League of Nations in 1923 and toured Europe in 1924, collecting ideas and allies. The old guard around the empress tried to push back and kept losing. In 1928 she crowned him negus, a king serving under her, which showed just how far her power had shrunk.

In 1930 her husband, Ras Gugsa Welle, rose against Tafari in the north. Tafari's modern army, with aircraft, beat him at Anchem, and Gugsa was killed on 31 March. Two days later, on 2 April, Zewditu died too.

claims.text: Zewditu died of shock and grief at the news of her husband's death.
claims.note: A popular story; other accounts say she was never told how the battle ended before she died.

claims.text: She died after being plunged into cold holy water to cure a fever.
claims.note: Reported by some foreign diplomats in Addis Ababa at the time; impossible to check.

claims.text: Tafari used aircraft against Gugsa Welle at Anchem.
claims.note: Standard histories describe his small air force bombing and scattering Gugsa's troops.

reigns.hook: Zewditu is dead and Tafari is ready. He takes a new name, Haile Selassie, "Power of the Trinity", and plans a coronation the whole world will notice.

reigns.tagline: The Lion of Judah who stood up to Mussolini
reigns.previously: Zewditu dies, two days after her rebel husband is killed.
paragraphs: Ras Tafari became Haile Selassie and was crowned on 2 November 1930 in front of a crowd of foreign guests. In 1931 he gave Ethiopia its first written constitution, though real power stayed firmly with him. Then Mussolini came. Italy invaded in October 1935, and in 1936 the emperor went into exile. In Geneva he begged the League of Nations to defend one of its members. It did nothing.

British and Ethiopian forces brought him home in 1941. For the next three decades he was Africa's elder statesman. Eritrea was federated with Ethiopia in 1952 and annexed in 1962. In 1963 he hosted the founding of the Organisation of African Unity in Addis Ababa. Rastafarians saw him as divine, and when he visited Jamaica in 1966 huge crowds swamped the airport.

At home, change crawled. A terrible famine in Wollo was hushed up until a British TV report exposed it in 1973. In 1974 strikes, student protests and army mutinies spread. On 12 September soldiers took the old emperor from his palace, and he died in custody in August 1975.

claims.text: Haile Selassie was murdered by the Derg.
claims.note: The Derg said he died after a prostate operation. Later trial evidence pointed to him being smothered, and his remains were found buried in the palace grounds in 1992.

claims.text: He was driven off to detention in a small Volkswagen.
claims.note: Reported by witnesses and journalists at the time; many saw it as a calculated humiliation.

reigns.title: The Italian Occupation
reigns.tagline: Five years under Mussolini's flag
reigns.reignEnded: Driven out by Allied and patriot forces
reigns.previously: Rewind to 1935. Italy invades and the emperor's armies give way.
paragraphs: Mussolini wanted an empire, and revenge for Italy's defeat at Adwa in 1896. His armies invaded in October 1935 with aircraft, tanks and poison gas, which was used on soldiers and civilians. Ethiopia's armies were broken one after another. Marshal Pietro Badoglio entered Addis Ababa on 5 May 1936, and Ethiopia was joined with Eritrea and Italian Somalia as Italian East Africa.

Occupation was brutal. After a grenade attack on the viceroy, Rodolfo Graziani, in February 1937, a date Ethiopians call Yekatit 12, Italian soldiers and civilians killed thousands of people in Addis Ababa over three days. Months later hundreds of monks and others were killed at the monastery of Debre Libanos. Across the highlands the Arbegnoch, the patriots, kept up a guerrilla war.

When Italy joined the Second World War in 1940, Britain backed the exiled emperor. British, Commonwealth and Ethiopian forces drove the Italians back, and on 5 May 1941, five years to the day after Badoglio's entry, Haile Selassie returned to his capital.

claims.text: Italy used poison gas in Ethiopia.
claims.note: Witnessed and reported at the time but denied in Italy for decades; the Italian government formally admitted it in 1996.

claims.text: Around 19,000 to 30,000 people were killed in the Yekatit 12 massacre.
claims.note: Ethiopian figures say about 30,000; Ian Campbell's study estimates around 19,000 to 20,000. Italian figures at the time were far lower.

reigns.hook: Fast forward to 1974. The emperor restored in 1941 is in his eighties, a famine has been covered up, and soldiers are about to make General Aman Andom their figurehead.

reigns.tagline: The Desert Lion the soldiers chose, then killed
reigns.cameToPower: Named Derg chairman by the soldiers
reigns.previously: Back to 1974: soldiers take Haile Selassie from his palace.
paragraphs: On 12 September 1974 a committee of soldiers took Haile Selassie from his palace. They called themselves the Derg, which means "committee". With no crown left to follow, this deck now tracks whoever held power. Three days later the Derg named its public face: Lieutenant General Aman Andom, as chairman and head of state.

Aman was a famous soldier. Born in Eritrea and schooled in Sudan, he came back with the British forces that drove out the Italians, served with Ethiopian troops in Korea and the Congo, and earned the nickname "Desert Lion" fighting Somalia in 1964. The Derg also named the absent Crown Prince Asfaw Wossen king, a title he never accepted.

Aman soon clashed with the junior officers who had picked him. He wanted a smaller Derg, talks with the Eritrean rebels, and no executions of jailed officials. He lost on all three. On 17 November he was dropped. On the night of 23 November troops attacked his house in Addis Ababa and he died in the shoot-out. That same night about sixty former officials were shot without trial.

claims.text: About sixty former officials were executed the night Aman died.
claims.note: The Derg announced the executions itself.

claims.text: Aman died resisting arrest.
claims.note: That was the Derg's account. Exactly how he died in the attack on his house is unclear.

claims.text: The Derg proclaimed Crown Prince Asfaw Wossen king.
claims.note: Announced when it took power. The prince, abroad after a stroke, never accepted, and the idea died with the monarchy in 1975.

reigns.hook: The Derg needs a new chairman, and this time it wants a quiet one. It picks Brigadier General Tafari Benti, while real power gathers around his deputy, Major Mengistu Haile Mariam.

reigns.tagline: The quiet general at the front of a revolution
reigns.previously: Aman Andom is killed, and about sixty officials are shot that night.
paragraphs: Brigadier General Tafari Benti (also spelled Teferi Bante) was an Oromo career officer, trained at the Holeta military academy, who had once served as military attaché in Washington. On 28 November 1974 the Derg made him its chairman and head of state. Colleagues saw him as a safe, neutral choice.

His time in office turned Ethiopia upside down. Students were sent into the countryside to spread the revolution. In March 1975 all rural land was nationalised and the monarchy was formally abolished. City land and rented houses followed that summer. Haile Selassie died in custody on 27 August 1975.

Behind the scenes the first vice-chairman, Mengistu Haile Mariam, was building his power. In December 1976 a reshuffle seemed to clip his wings, and Tafari began speaking up for working with the civilian left. On 3 February 1977 a gunfight broke out at a Derg meeting. Tafari and several others were killed.

claims.text: The December 1976 reorganisation was meant to curb Mengistu.
claims.note: René Lefort and others read it that way. What Tafari himself intended is unclear.

claims.text: Mengistu personally opened fire at the February 1977 meeting.
claims.note: Often told, but accounts of who fired first and who did the killing contradict each other.

claims.text: The monarchy was formally abolished in March 1975.
claims.note: Proclaimed by the Derg itself.

reigns.hook: Mengistu Haile Mariam comes out of the gunfight as master of the Derg. Within days he is its chairman, and a campaign of terror against his enemies is about to begin.

reigns.tagline: The Marxist strongman of the Red Terror
reigns.cameToPower: Won a shoot-out inside the Derg
reigns.previously: Tafari Benti dies in a gunfight inside the Derg. Mengistu is on top.
paragraphs: Mengistu Haile Mariam was an army officer of modest background who made himself master of the Derg. In 1977 and 1978 his regime waged the Red Terror against rival leftist groups and anyone suspected of opposing it. Young people were killed in the streets and their bodies left on show. Tens of thousands died at the very least; the true toll is unknown and disputed.

Somalia invaded the Ogaden in 1977, and with Soviet weapons and Cuban troops Ethiopia drove it out by March 1978. The wars against rebels in Eritrea and Tigray dragged on for years. The famine of 1983 to 1985 killed hundreds of thousands, and TV reports from the camps led to Band Aid and Live Aid. In 1987 Ethiopia became a People's Democratic Republic, with Mengistu as president.

As Soviet help dried up, the rebels closed in. On 21 May 1991 Mengistu flew to Zimbabwe, where he has lived ever since. An Ethiopian court convicted him of genocide in his absence in 2006, and an appeal in 2008 turned his life sentence into a death sentence.

claims.text: Mengistu was convicted of genocide by an Ethiopian court in his absence.
claims.note: Verdict delivered in December 2006 after a trial lasting more than a decade.

claims.text: He has lived in Zimbabwe since May 1991.
claims.note: Given asylum under Robert Mugabe; Zimbabwe has not extradited him.

claims.text: Cuban troops helped Ethiopia win the Ogaden War.
claims.note: Thousands of Cuban soldiers and Soviet advisers fought on Ethiopia's side in 1977 to 1978.

reigns.relationToPredecessor: Mengistu's vice president and old pal

reigns.previously: Mengistu flies off to Zimbabwe as rebel armies close on the capital.
paragraphs: Tesfaye Gebre Kidan started out as a village schoolteacher, quit over the poor pay and joined the army. At the Holetta military academy he got to know Mengistu Haile Mariam, and he stayed in the inner circle for good. A Derg member, he led troops around Jijiga in the Ogaden War, served for years as defence minister, ran Eritrea as military governor from 1988 and was made vice president in April 1991.

When Mengistu flew out on 21 May, Tesfaye was left holding a government with no army worth the name. Units turned on each other and soldiers looted whatever they could carry. He told the American chargé d'affaires he had lost control, announced a ceasefire and ran for the Italian embassy. Within a week the EPRDF rebels were in the capital.

He never left the embassy compound. He spent thirteen years there with other former Derg men, suffered a stroke and ended up in a wheelchair. His death was confirmed in June 2004, and how it happened is still argued over.

claims.text: Tesfaye asked the US embassy for shelter first and was turned away.
claims.note: Told by the historian Paul Henze; the Italian embassy is the one that took him in, and stories of the night vary.

claims.text: He died after a fellow refugee, ex-foreign minister Berhanu Bayeh, hit him with a bottle.
claims.note: A waiter's account in an Italian book; an embassy source told CNN that Berhanu was not involved.

claims.text: He lived the rest of his life inside the Italian embassy in Addis Ababa.
claims.note: He sheltered there from May 1991 until his death in 2004, with other Derg officials Ethiopia wanted to try.

reigns.hook: Tesfaye is hiding behind Italian walls and the old army has melted away. Rebel columns from the north, led by a former medical student from Tigray named Meles Zenawi, roll into Addis Ababa.

reigns.tagline: The guerrilla who wanted Ethiopia to grow like Asia
reigns.cameToPower: His rebel army took the capital
reigns.previously: Acting president Tesfaye gives up and runs for the Italian embassy.
paragraphs: Meles Zenawi left medical school in 1975 to fight with the Tigray People's Liberation Front. Born Legesse, he took the name Meles from a student comrade executed by the Derg. By 1991 he led the EPRDF, a rebel coalition built around the TPLF, and on 28 May its fighters entered Addis Ababa. He became president of the transitional government, then prime minister in 1995.

He rebuilt the state along ethnic lines, giving each big group its own region and, on paper, a right to secede. Eritrea voted for independence in 1993. Five years later a border quarrel became a full war with Eritrea, fought from 1998 to 2000 at a huge cost in lives. The disputed 2005 election ended in street protests and a crackdown in which nearly 200 people were killed.

Meles was a sharp thinker who wanted a state-led boom on the East Asian model, and the economy grew fast for years. Critics said the country had become a one-party state in all but name. He fell ill in 2012 and died in Brussels on 20 August, still in office.

claims.text: Meles took his name in honour of an executed fellow student.
claims.note: Meles Tekle was executed by the Derg in 1975; Legesse Zenawi adopted his name as a fighter.

claims.text: Ethiopia's economy grew by around 10 percent a year under Meles.
claims.note: Those were the official figures for much of the 2000s; some outside economists thought the true rate was lower.

claims.text: The government kept his final illness secret.
claims.note: Officials said he was recovering until his death was announced, and the illness was never officially named.

reigns.hook: Meles is dead and no one had planned for it. The job goes to his quiet deputy, an engineer from the south who is not from Tigray at all.

reigns.tagline: The quiet engineer who chose to walk away
reigns.previously: Meles Zenawi dies in office in Brussels, aged 57.
paragraphs: Hailemariam Desalegn was a civil engineer from Wolayita in the south, trained in Addis Ababa and Finland, who ran a water technology institute before going into politics. He was not from Tigray and belonged to a small Pentecostal church, an outsider in a coalition long dominated by the TPLF. When Meles died in August 2012 he took over, first as acting prime minister.

He promised to carry on Meles's plans, from giant dams to industrial parks, and chaired the African Union in 2013 to 2014. From 2015 protests spread across Oromia, set off by plans to expand Addis Ababa onto Oromo farmland, and then into Amhara. Hundreds were killed in crackdowns, and a state of emergency was declared in October 2016.

On 15 February 2018 he announced his resignation, saying he wanted to clear the way for reform. It was a rare thing in Ethiopia: a leader leaving office alive and by choice. He stayed on until the ruling coalition's new leader was sworn in on 2 April.

claims.text: He was the first modern Ethiopian ruler to step down voluntarily.
claims.note: Every leader before him since the 19th century died in office, was deposed or fled.

claims.text: Security forces killed hundreds of protesters in 2015 and 2016.
claims.note: Documented by Human Rights Watch and by Ethiopia's own human rights commission.

reigns.hook: The ruling coalition needs a new face, fast. It picks a young Oromo former army officer who promises to open the prisons and make peace with Eritrea.

reigns.tagline: From Nobel peacemaker to wartime prime minister
reigns.previously: Hailemariam resigns, a rare voluntary exit amid mass protests.
paragraphs: Abiy Ahmed was born in 1976 to an Oromo Muslim father and an Amhara Christian mother. He fought against the Derg as a teenager and rose through the army and intelligence services. He became prime minister in April 2018 as leader of the ruling EPRDF. Within months he freed thousands of political prisoners, lifted bans on opposition groups and made peace with Eritrea, winning the 2019 Nobel Peace Prize.

In 2019 he merged the EPRDF into his new Prosperity Party; the TPLF refused to join. In November 2020 war broke out in Tigray, drawing in Eritrean troops. Fighting, atrocities and hunger killed a very large number of people; estimates run into the hundreds of thousands and are disputed. The Pretoria agreement of November 2022 ended the war.

Armed conflict went on in Amhara, with the Fano militias, and in Oromia. Abiy pushed through the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Blue Nile, opened in September 2025 despite Egypt's fierce objections. In the general election of 1 June 2026, with no voting in Tigray, the Prosperity Party won a large majority, and Abiy remains prime minister.

claims.text: Abiy won the 2019 Nobel Peace Prize for ending the standoff with Eritrea.
claims.note: The Norwegian Nobel Committee's citation named his initiative to settle the border conflict with Eritrea.

claims.text: The Pretoria agreement ended the Tigray war in November 2022.
claims.note: Signed on 2 November 2022 by the federal government and the TPLF, with African Union mediation.

claims.text: No voting took place in Tigray in the June 2026 election.
claims.note: The National Election Board of Ethiopia cited conditions in the region after the war.
